# Body & Anatomy

## The Vulva — External Anatomy.

*The vulva is the collective name for all female external genitalia. Many people use "vagina" to mean all of this, but the vagina is internal. The vulva is what you see on the outside. Every vulva is unique in size, shape, colour and symmetry — variation is completely normal and beautiful.*

---

### Mons Pubis

The fatty, rounded area above the pubic bone, covered with pubic hair after puberty. Provides cushioning during activities and protects the pubic bone. Pubic hair removal is a personal choice, not a medical necessity — shaving or waxing can increase the risk of irritation, ingrown hairs and folliculitis.

---

### Labia Majora (Outer Lips)

Two fleshy folds from the mons pubis to the perineum containing fatty tissue, sweat and oil glands. Outer surface is pigmented with pubic hair; inner surface is smooth. **Primary role:** protect the more delicate inner structures from friction, injury and pathogens. The female homologue of the scrotum. May shrink slightly after menopause as oestrogen declines.

---

### Labia Minora (Inner Lips)

Two thin, hairless folds inside the outer lips — highly variable in appearance. Made of **erectile tissue** (no fat), they swell and may darken during arousal. Densely packed with nerve endings. They split at the top to form the **clitoral hood (prepuce)** and frenulum; meet at the bottom at the posterior fourchette. Asymmetry between sides is completely normal and common.

---

### Clitoris — The Full Structure

Much larger than the visible glans. It is a wishbone-shaped organ with:

- **Glans** (visible tip, ~8,000 nerve endings — more than any other human structure)
- **Body** (extends internally beneath the hood)
- **Crura/Legs** (two wings hugging the urethra and vagina internally)
- **Vestibular bulbs**

Its only known purpose is pleasure. Develops from the same embryonic tissue as the penis.

---

### Urethral Opening (Meatus)

The tiny hole below the clitoris and above the vaginal opening where urine exits. **NOT** part of the reproductive system. Female urethra is only ~4 cm long (vs 20 cm in males) — this short distance explains why women are far more prone to UTIs. You cannot insert a tampon into the urethra — it is far too small. Urine and menstrual products exit through separate channels.

---

### Vaginal Opening & Hymen

The entrance to the vaginal canal, surrounded by the **hymen** — a thin, stretchy membrane that varies enormously between individuals (crescent, ring, fringed, or very small). It can stretch from exercise, tampon use or medical exams. Its presence does **NOT** indicate sexual history. Some people are born without a hymen. First penetration may or may not cause discomfort or bleeding — both are normal.

---

### Bartholin's Glands

Two pea-sized glands at the 4 o'clock and 8 o'clock positions near the vaginal opening. Not active until puberty. Produce lubrication during arousal. Usually unnoticed when healthy. Can become blocked forming a painless **cyst**, or infected forming a painful **abscess** (swollen, tender lump making sitting/walking difficult — requires drainage by a healthcare provider).

---

### Skene's Glands (Paraurethral)

Two small glands on either side of the lower end of the urethra, sometimes called the "female prostate" due to functional similarities. They produce fluid into the urethra during arousal, believed to contribute to lubrication and female ejaculation. Their tiny ducts are vulnerable to ascending bacteria — blockage or infection causes **skenitis**.

---

💡 **Key Point**

The vulva does not need special products to be "clean." Warm water and gentle care are all that is required. Less is more. Harsh soaps, douches, vaginal sprays and vaginal steaming cause irritation and disrupt natural balance — there is no evidence any of them benefit health.

---

## Vulva Hygiene: Daily Do's & Don'ts

### ✅ Do

- Wash the external vulva once daily with warm water only, or a very mild, fragrance-free pH-balanced intimate cleanser
- Wipe from front to back after using the toilet — this prevents E. coli reaching the urethra or vagina
- Pat gently dry with a clean soft towel (avoid rubbing)
- Wear breathable cotton underwear during the day; avoid wearing underwear to bed
- Change out of wet clothing (swimsuits, gym wear) promptly — moisture breeds yeast and bacteria
- Change sanitary products regularly as per instructions

---

### 🚫 Never

- Douche — it disrupts healthy bacteria and increases infection risk
- Use scented soaps, bubble baths, sprays or wipes on the vulva
- Use scented tampons or pads
- Attempt vaginal steaming — no proven benefits, risk of serious burns and flora disruption
- Wear tight, non-breathable fabrics for prolonged periods
- Flush used pads or tampons — wrap and bin them

---

## Common Vulvar Conditions

| Condition | Key Symptoms | Action |
|-----------|-------------|--------|
| **Vulvitis** | Redness, swelling, itching, burning — caused by irritants, infections or allergies | Identify and remove trigger; see provider if persistent |
| **Bartholin's Abscess** | Tender, hot, swollen painful lump near vaginal opening; makes sitting/walking difficult | See provider promptly — requires drainage |
| **Vulvodynia** | Chronic, unexplained burning, stinging, rawness or pain lasting ≥3 months with no identifiable cause | Requires specialist evaluation — treatable |
| **Contact Dermatitis** | Itching, burning, red rash — allergic or irritant reaction (soaps, detergents, lubricants) | Remove the irritant; antihistamines or corticosteroids if needed |
| **Genital Warts (HPV)** | Flesh-coloured, cauliflower-like bumps on vulva or perianal area | See provider — treatable; HPV vaccine prevents most cases |
| **Herpes** | Painful, fluid-filled blisters or open sores; tingling or burning before outbreak | See provider — antiviral treatment reduces outbreaks |
| **Lichen Sclerosus** | White, thin skin patches; intense itching; may cause scarring — increases vulvar cancer risk | Regular follow-up with gynaecologist essential |

---

## The Vagina — Internal Canal

*The vagina is a stretchy, self-cleaning fibromuscular canal connecting the cervix to the outside world. It serves menstruation, sexual function, conception and childbirth. It is not the same as the vulva — the vagina is purely internal.*

---

### The Three Layers of the Vaginal Wall

**1. Mucosal Layer (Inner)**

Similar to skin but without glands. Produces moisture via **transudation** (fluid seeping through walls). Contains **rugae** — transverse folds like pleats that allow dramatic stretching during sex and childbirth. Hosts **Lactobacillus** bacteria that produce lactic acid maintaining protective pH 3.8–4.5.

**2. Muscular Layer (Middle)**

Smooth muscle that contracts and expands. Helps expel discharge and menstrual fluid. Surrounded and supported by the pelvic floor muscles — pelvic floor health directly affects vaginal function.

**3. Adventitia Layer (Outer)**

Connective tissue rich in collagen and elastic fibres. Anchors the vagina to surrounding pelvic structures (bladder, rectum, urethra). Allows expansion and recoil. The slightly acidic discharge that can bleach dark underwear is completely normal — it's the vaginal flora doing their job.

---

💡 **The Vagina is Self-Cleaning**

The vaginal flora — healthy bacteria naturally living in the vagina — are your first line of defence. They maintain an acidic pH that prevents harmful bacteria and yeast from overgrowing. Douching, scented products and vaginal steaming disrupt this system. The vagina is like the eye — it cleans itself and needs no internal washing.

---

## Vaginal Infections — The Three Main Types

| Infection | Cause | Key Signs | Treatment |
|-----------|-------|----------|-----------|
| **Bacterial Vaginosis (BV)** *Most common cause of vaginal discharge* | Overgrowth of harmful bacteria, decrease in Lactobacilli. Triggered by douching, new/multiple sex partners, no condoms. **NOT an STI** but sexual activity can trigger it. | Thin, grey or white discharge; strong fishy odour (especially after sex); mild itching or burning | Prescription antibiotics (metronidazole or clindamycin). Partner does not need treatment for first episode. |
| **Yeast Infection (Candidiasis)** *Candida albicans overgrowth* | Overgrowth of Candida fungus. Risk factors: antibiotic use (kills healthy bacteria), high oestrogen (pregnancy, HRT), uncontrolled diabetes, weakened immune system (HIV/AIDS) | Thick, white, cottage-cheese-like discharge; intense itching; redness and swelling of vulva; burning during urination or sex | Over-the-counter antifungal creams or suppositories (if confirmed). See provider if first time, pregnant, or recurrent. |
| **Trichomoniasis ("Trich")** *STI — Trichomonas vaginalis parasite* | Sexually transmitted parasite. Many people have NO symptoms and unknowingly spread it. Both partners must be tested and treated. | Frothy, yellow-green discharge with strong odour; itching and redness; pain during urination or sex; lower abdominal discomfort | Prescription antibiotics (metronidazole). **Both partners must be treated** to prevent reinfection. |
| **Vaginal Atrophy (GSM)** *Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause* | Thinning, drying and inflammation of vaginal walls due to decreased oestrogen — most common during menopause or breastfeeding | Vaginal dryness, burning, decreased lubrication, pain during sex, urinary urgency, recurrent UTIs | Vaginal moisturizers (first-line), lubricants, low-dose vaginal oestrogen (prescription), ospemifene tablets |

---

⚠️ **Critical Warning**

Vaginal symptoms often overlap — yeast infection, BV and trichomoniasis can all cause itching and discharge but require completely different treatments. **Self-diagnosis is unreliable.** Do not use over-the-counter antifungal creams if you're not certain it's a yeast infection — using them for BV or trichomoniasis will not work and will delay proper treatment.

---

## Kenya Myth-Busting: Vaginal Health

| ❌ Myth | ✅ Truth |
|--------|---------|
| "The vagina must be washed inside to stay clean" | The vagina is self-cleaning. Its discharge and healthy bacteria keep it balanced. Internal washing (douching) removes good bacteria and increases infection risk. |
| "If there's no smell, there's no infection" | Many infections including chlamydia, gonorrhoea and early trichomoniasis often have NO symptoms. You cannot rely on smell or appearance alone. |
| "Pain during sex is normal for women" | Persistent pain during intercourse (dyspareunia) is a medical symptom, not a normal part of being a woman. It requires evaluation. |
| "Vaginal steaming cleanses the womb" | No evidence supports this. Steaming can cause serious burns to vaginal walls and disrupt healthy flora, leading to infections. |
| "The hymen determines virginity" | The hymen is a stretchy membrane with natural variation. It can be stretched by many non-sexual activities. It does not prove sexual history. |
| "Public toilets can give you an STI" | Most STI pathogens are fragile and cannot survive on toilet seats. They require close skin-to-skin or fluid contact for transmission. |

---

## The Cervix — The Gatekeeper

*The cervix is the lower, cylindrical part of the uterus that connects the uterine body to the vagina. Approximately 4 cm long and 3 cm in diameter. It is not a separate organ — it's an integral part of the uterus, acting as passageway, protective barrier and producer of critical fluids.*

### Four Critical Functions

**1. Gatekeeper for sperm:** Thick plug-like mucus most of the month; around ovulation becomes thin, clear and stretchy (egg-white) creating a sperm-friendly environment.

**2. Protective barrier:** Remains tightly closed during pregnancy.

**3. Childbirth pathway:** Softens, effaces and dilates to ~10 cm during labour.

**4. Menstrual passage:** Allows menstrual blood to exit.

---

### The Transformation Zone — Why It Matters

The cervix has two cell types: **Glandular cells** (columnar, line the canal, produce mucus — reddish velvet appearance) and **Squamous cells** (flat, protective, cover the ectocervix — smooth pink). Where they meet is the **transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction)** — the most common site for cervical cancer to develop. This is why Pap smears target this area specifically. Its location shifts with age and hormones.

✨ **Cervix Changes You Can Track**

The cervix changes texture and position throughout your menstrual cycle. Around ovulation it becomes **softer, higher and more open** (like pursed lips) to allow sperm entry. After ovulation it becomes **firmer, lower and closed**. Tracking these changes is a valid form of fertility awareness.

---

## Cervical Screening — Kenya Guidelines

| Test | What It Detects | When & How Often |
|------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Pap Smear** | Abnormal cell changes on the cervix that could potentially become cancer | Ages 21–25: every 3 years; Ages 25–65: every 3 years (preferred) or co-test with HPV every 5 years |
| **HPV Test** | High-risk HPV types (especially 16 & 18) that cause cell changes | Ages 26–65: every 5 years (preferred method); can be self-collected |
| **Co-testing** | Both HPV + Pap together | Every 5 years, ages 25–65 |
| **HIV-positive women** | Pap smear every year from age 21 | Annual — HIV increases cervical cancer risk significantly |

🇰🇪 **Kenya Context**

Kenya transitioned to a **single-dose HPV vaccination schedule in November 2025**, making it easier to reach more girls. The HPV vaccine is free of charge at public health facilities for girls aged 10 years. Research by Kenyan doctors — Dr. Nelly Mugo, Dr. Elizabeth Bukusi, Dr. Maricianah Onono and Dr. Betty Njoroge through the KENSHE study (KEMRI/University of Washington) — was instrumental in establishing single-dose efficacy globally.

---

## Uterus, Fallopian Tubes & Ovaries

---

### The Uterus (Womb)

A hollow, pear-shaped muscular organ — the central anatomical landmark of the female internal genitalia. Before pregnancy it is ~7–8 cm long. During pregnancy it expands to the ribcage and can weigh up to 1 kg. After menopause it atrophies and shrinks back down. About 80% of uteri are **"anteverted"** (tilted forward toward the bladder); others are **"retroverted"** (tilted backward) — both are normal variations, not problems.

**Three Layers of the Uterine Wall**

**Perimetrium:** Thin outer serous membrane covering the uterus.

**Myometrium:** The thick middle muscular layer — powerfully contracts during menstruation and labour. Where fibroids grow.

**Endometrium:** The inner mucosal layer with two sublayers — the permanent *basal layer* and the *functional layer* that thickens and sheds monthly.

**Four Parts of the Uterus**

**Fundus:** Broad, curved top above the fallopian tube openings.

**Body (Corpus):** Main central portion where most of the organ is.

**Isthmus:** Narrowed lower neck just above the cervix.

**Cervix:** The lower cylindrical part connecting to the vagina (detailed above).

Held in place by broad, round and uterosacral ligaments.

**Three Key Functions**

**1. Menstruation:** Each month, the endometrium thickens in preparation for potential pregnancy; sheds if no fertilisation occurs.

**2. Implantation & fetal development:** A fertilised egg implants into the nutrient-rich endometrium; the uterus becomes the fetus's home throughout pregnancy.

**3. Labour & delivery:** Myometrial contractions dilate the cervix and push the baby through the birth canal.

---

### The Fallopian Tubes — Where Fertilisation Happens

Two narrow, muscular canals (~11–12 cm long) connecting the ovaries to the uterus. The tubes are *not* directly attached to the ovaries — they have finger-like projections called **fimbriae** that reach out to sweep the egg into the tube at ovulation. The tubes are alive with movement: cilia create a current and muscular walls contract to transport egg, sperm and embryo.

**Four Regions of Each Tube**

**Intramural:** The shortest, narrowest section passing through the uterine wall.

**Isthmus:** Narrow segment next to the uterus.

**Ampulla:** The longest, widest part — most common site of fertilisation. Has folded lining for increased surface area.

**Infundibulum:** The funnel-shaped open end near the ovary, fringed with fimbriae.

**Tubal Conditions**

**Salpingitis/PID:** Infection (usually chlamydia/gonorrhoea) causing inflammation, often with no symptoms. Can scar and block tubes, causing infertility.

**Hydrosalpinx:** Fluid-filled blocked tube — often from prior infection; causes infertility.

**Ectopic Pregnancy:** Fertilised egg implants in the tube instead of the uterus — a **medical emergency**. Symptoms: sudden sharp one-sided pain, vaginal bleeding, shoulder tip pain, dizziness. Requires immediate care.

**Tubal factor infertility:** Accounts for up to one-third of infertility cases.

---

### The Ovaries — Hormonal Architects

Two small, oval-shaped organs (~3.5 × 2 × 1 cm in reproductive years; shrink after menopause) — the female equivalent of the testes. They have two essential roles: producing eggs and secreting hormones.

**Egg Production — A Finite Resource**

You are born with all the eggs you will ever have: ~6–7 million in utero, ~1–2 million at birth, ~300,000 at puberty. Only 300–400 will ever be ovulated. The rest naturally degenerate through **atresia**. You cannot make new eggs. This is why age-related fertility decline is real — both egg quantity and quality decrease over time.

**Hormones the Ovaries Produce**

**Estrogen:** Develops secondary sex characteristics, thickens the uterine lining, maintains bone density, skin health, mood.

**Progesterone:** Prepares the uterine lining for implantation; dominant in the second half of the cycle; maintains early pregnancy.

**Testosterone:** Yes — women produce testosterone in small amounts; plays roles in libido, mood and muscle mass.

**Inhibin:** Regulates FSH production in the pituitary.

⚠️ **Seek Urgent Care If:**

Sudden, severe, one-sided pelvic pain could indicate **ovarian torsion** (twisting of the ovary on its ligaments, cutting off blood supply) or a **ruptured ovarian cyst** — both are medical emergencies. Pain accompanied by fever, nausea/vomiting or faintness requires immediate attention. Heavy bleeding with pain, or bleeding combined with a positive pregnancy test, also warrant urgent evaluation.

---

## The Urethra — Urinary Pathway

*The urethra is a narrow tube (~4 cm long) connecting the urinary bladder to the outside. Its primary job is urine elimination — it is NOT part of the reproductive system. However, because of its close proximity to the vagina and anus, it is deeply connected to pelvic health.*

### Structure: Three Layers

**Mucosal layer (inner):** Lined with transitional epithelium near the bladder, squamous near the opening. Contains folds allowing stretching.

**Spongy layer (submucosa):** Rich in blood vessels and elastic fibres; helps seal the urethra closed when not in use.

**Muscular layer (outer):** Smooth muscle fibres plus the external sphincter (voluntary control).

### Two Sphincters Control Urination

**Internal urethral sphincter:** Involuntary — opens automatically when the bladder is full.

**External urethral sphincter:** Voluntary — you control this to hold urine or let it out. Supported by the pelvic floor muscles.

The sensation "I need to pee" is triggered by **stretch receptors in the bladder wall**, not the urethra, when the bladder is about half full.

---

## UTI — Urinary Tract Infection

A UTI is **not an STI** — it is a completely separate system. Most commonly caused by E. coli from the digestive tract entering the urethra. The short female urethra (~4 cm vs 20 cm in males) is why women are far more prone.

| Symptom | Risk Factor | Prevention |
|---------|------------|-----------|
| Pain or burning during urination (dysuria) | Wiping back to front (brings bacteria forward) | **Always wipe front to back** — single most important hygiene habit |
| Frequent urge to urinate, passing only small amounts | Holding urine for too long | Urinate when you feel the urge; don't hold it |
| Cloudy, dark or bloody urine | Sexual activity ("honeymoon cystitis" — bacteria pushed into urethra during intercourse) | **Urinate after sex** — one of the most effective prevention strategies |
| Strong-smelling urine | Menopause (low oestrogen thins urethral tissues, reducing defences) | Stay hydrated — dilutes urine and flushes bacteria |
| Pelvic pressure or incomplete emptying | Spermicides or diaphragms | Wear breathable cotton underwear; avoid tight synthetics |

🚨 **Seek Urgent Care — Signs the Infection Has Reached the Kidneys**

**Fever, chills or shaking · Nausea or vomiting · Pain in your back or side (flank pain, just below ribs) · Inability to urinate · Visibly bloody urine (red or pink)**

These indicate **pyelonephritis** (kidney infection) — a more serious condition requiring immediate treatment. A simple lower UTI often has NO fever — do not wait for fever to seek care.

---

## Kenya Myth-Busting: Urinary Health

| ❌ Myth | ✅ Truth |
|--------|---------|
| "Drinking less water will reduce the burning" | Burning is caused by inflammation, not water volume. Drinking less concentrates urine, making burning worse. Drinking more helps dilute and flush bacteria. |
| "If I have a UTI, I will always have a fever" | A simple lower UTI (urethritis/cystitis) often causes NO fever. Fever signals the infection has moved up to the kidneys — a more serious condition. You can be very sick with a UTI without early fever. |
| "You can stop antibiotics once the burning stops" | Dangerous. Stopping early leaves the strongest bacteria behind, creating a resistant recurrent infection. Always finish the full prescribed course.

## The Vulva — External Anatomy

*The vulva is the collective name for all female external genitalia. Many people use "vagina" to mean all of this, but the vagina is internal. The vulva is what you see on the outside. Every vulva is unique in size, shape, colour and symmetry — variation is completely normal and beautiful.*

---

### Mons Pubis

The fatty, rounded area above the pubic bone, covered with pubic hair after puberty. Provides cushioning during activities and protects the pubic bone. Pubic hair removal is a personal choice, not a medical necessity — shaving or waxing can increase the risk of irritation, ingrown hairs and folliculitis.

---

### Labia Majora (Outer Lips)

Two fleshy folds from the mons pubis to the perineum containing fatty tissue, sweat and oil glands. Outer surface is pigmented with pubic hair; inner surface is smooth. **Primary role:** protect the more delicate inner structures from friction, injury and pathogens. The female homologue of the scrotum. May shrink slightly after menopause as oestrogen declines.

---

### Labia Minora (Inner Lips)

Two thin, hairless folds inside the outer lips — highly variable in appearance. Made of **erectile tissue** (no fat), they swell and may darken during arousal. Densely packed with nerve endings. They split at the top to form the **clitoral hood (prepuce)** and frenulum; meet at the bottom at the posterior fourchette. Asymmetry between sides is completely normal and common.

---

### Clitoris (The Full Structure)

Much larger than the visible glans. It is a wishbone-shaped organ with:
- **Glans** (visible tip, ~8,000 nerve endings — more than any other human structure)
- **Body** (extends internally beneath the hood)
- **Crura/Legs** (two wings hugging the urethra and vagina internally)
- **Vestibular bulbs** Its only known purpose is pleasure. Develops from the same embryonic tissue as the penis.

---

### Urethral Opening (Meatus)

The tiny hole below the clitoris and above the vaginal opening where urine exits. **NOT** part of the reproductive system. Female urethra is only ~4 cm long (vs 20 cm in males) — this short distance explains why women are far more prone to UTIs. You cannot insert a tampon into the urethra — it is far too small. Urine and menstrual products exit through separate channels.

---

### Vaginal Opening & Hymen

The entrance to the vaginal canal, surrounded by the **hymen** — a thin, stretchy membrane that varies enormously between individuals (crescent, ring, fringed, or very small). It can stretch from exercise, tampon use or medical exams. Its presence does **NOT** indicate sexual history. Some people are born without a hymen. First penetration may or may not cause discomfort or bleeding — both are normal.

---

### Bartholin's Glands

Two pea-sized glands at the 4 o'clock and 8 o'clock positions near the vaginal opening. Not active until puberty. Produce lubrication during arousal. Usually unnoticed when healthy. Can become blocked forming a painless **cyst**, or infected forming a painful **abscess** (swollen, tender lump making sitting/walking difficult — requires drainage by a healthcare provider).

---

### Skene's Glands (Paraurethral)

Two small glands on either side of the lower end of the urethra, sometimes called the "female prostate" due to functional similarities. They produce fluid into the urethra during arousal, believed to contribute to lubrication and female ejaculation. Their tiny ducts are vulnerable to ascending bacteria — blockage or infection causes **skenitis**.

---

💡 **Key Point**

The vulva does not need special products to be "clean." Warm water and gentle care are all that is required. Less is more. Harsh soaps, douches, vaginal sprays and vaginal steaming cause irritation and disrupt natural balance — there is no evidence any of them benefit health.

---

## Vulva Hygiene: Daily Do's & Don'ts

### ✅ Do

- Wash the external vulva once daily with warm water only, or a very mild, fragrance-free pH-balanced intimate cleanser
- Wipe from front to back after using the toilet — this prevents E. coli reaching the urethra or vagina
- Pat gently dry with a clean soft towel (avoid rubbing)
- Wear breathable cotton underwear during the day; avoid wearing underwear to bed
- Change out of wet clothing (swimsuits, gym wear) promptly — moisture breeds yeast and bacteria
- Change sanitary products regularly as per instructions

---

### 🚫 Never

- Douche — it disrupts healthy bacteria and increases infection risk
- Use scented soaps, bubble baths, sprays or wipes on the vulva
- Use scented tampons or pads
- Attempt vaginal steaming — no proven benefits, risk of serious burns and flora disruption
- Wear tight, non-breathable fabrics for prolonged periods
- Flush used pads or tampons — wrap and bin them

---

## Common Vulvar Conditions

| Condition | Key Symptoms | Action |
|-----------|-------------|--------|
| **Vulvitis** | Redness, swelling, itching, burning — caused by irritants, infections or allergies | Identify and remove trigger; see provider if persistent |
| **Bartholin's Abscess** | Tender, hot, swollen painful lump near vaginal opening; makes sitting/walking difficult | See provider promptly — requires drainage |
| **Vulvodynia** | Chronic, unexplained burning, stinging, rawness or pain lasting ≥3 months with no identifiable cause | Requires specialist evaluation — treatable |
| **Contact Dermatitis** | Itching, burning, red rash — allergic or irritant reaction (soaps, detergents, lubricants) | Remove the irritant; antihistamines or corticosteroids if needed |
| **Genital Warts (HPV)** | Flesh-coloured, cauliflower-like bumps on vulva or perianal area | See provider — treatable; HPV vaccine prevents most cases |
| **Herpes** | Painful, fluid-filled blisters or open sores; tingling or burning before outbreak | See provider — antiviral treatment reduces outbreaks |
| **Lichen Sclerosus** | White, thin skin patches; intense itching; may cause scarring — increases vulvar cancer risk | Regular follow-up with gynaecologist essential |

---

# The Vagina — Internal Canal

*The vagina is a stretchy, self-cleaning fibromuscular canal connecting the cervix to the outside world. It serves menstruation, sexual function, conception and childbirth. It is not the same as the vulva — the vagina is purely internal.*

---

## The Three Layers of the Vaginal Wall

### 1. Mucosal Layer (Inner)

Similar to skin but without glands. Produces moisture via **transudation** (fluid seeping through walls). Contains **rugae** — transverse folds like pleats that allow dramatic stretching during sex and childbirth. Hosts **Lactobacillus** bacteria that produce lactic acid maintaining protective pH 3.8–4.5.

### 2. Muscular Layer (Middle)

Smooth muscle that contracts and expands. Helps expel discharge and menstrual fluid. Surrounded and supported by the pelvic floor muscles — pelvic floor health directly affects vaginal function.

### 3. Adventitia Layer (Outer)

Connective tissue rich in collagen and elastic fibres. Anchors the vagina to surrounding pelvic structures (bladder, rectum, urethra). Allows expansion and recoil. The slightly acidic discharge that can bleach dark underwear is completely normal — it's the vaginal flora doing their job.

---

💡 **The Vagina is Self-Cleaning**

The vaginal flora — healthy bacteria naturally living in the vagina — are your first line of defence. They maintain an acidic pH that prevents harmful bacteria and yeast from overgrowing. Douching, scented products and vaginal steaming disrupt this system. The vagina is like the eye — it cleans itself and needs no internal washing.

---

## Vaginal Infections

### The Three Main Types

| Infection | Cause | Key Signs | Treatment |
|-----------|-------|----------|-----------|
| **Bacterial Vaginosis (BV)** *Most common cause of vaginal discharge* | Overgrowth of harmful bacteria, decrease in Lactobacilli. Triggered by douching, new/multiple sex partners, no condoms. **NOT an STI** but sexual activity can trigger it. | Thin, grey or white discharge; strong fishy odour (especially after sex); mild itching or burning | Prescription antibiotics (metronidazole or clindamycin). Partner does not need treatment for first episode. |
| **Yeast Infection (Candidiasis)** *Candida albicans overgrowth* | Overgrowth of Candida fungus. Risk factors: antibiotic use (kills healthy bacteria), high oestrogen (pregnancy, HRT), uncontrolled diabetes, weakened immune system (HIV/AIDS) | Thick, white, cottage-cheese-like discharge; intense itching; redness and swelling of vulva; burning during urination or sex | Over-the-counter antifungal creams or suppositories (if confirmed). See provider if first time, pregnant, or recurrent. |
| **Trichomoniasis ("Trich")** *STI — Trichomonas vaginalis parasite* | Sexually transmitted parasite. Many people have NO symptoms and unknowingly spread it. Both partners must be tested and treated. | Frothy, yellow-green discharge with strong odour; itching and redness; pain during urination or sex; lower abdominal discomfort | Prescription antibiotics (metronidazole). **Both partners must be treated** to prevent reinfection. |
| **Vaginal Atrophy (GSM)** *Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause* | Thinning, drying and inflammation of vaginal walls due to decreased oestrogen — most common during menopause or breastfeeding | Vaginal dryness, burning, decreased lubrication, pain during sex, urinary urgency, recurrent UTIs | Vaginal moisturizers (first-line), lubricants, low-dose vaginal oestrogen (prescription), ospemifene tablets |

---

⚠️ **Critical Warning**

Vaginal symptoms often overlap — yeast infection, BV and trichomoniasis can all cause itching and discharge but require completely different treatments. **Self-diagnosis is unreliable.** Do not use over-the-counter antifungal creams if you're not certain it's a yeast infection — using them for BV or trichomoniasis will not work and will delay proper treatment.

---

## Kenya Myth-Busting: Vaginal Health

| ❌ Myth | ✅ Truth |
|--------|---------|
| "The vagina must be washed inside to stay clean" | The vagina is self-cleaning. Its discharge and healthy bacteria keep it balanced. Internal washing (douching) removes good bacteria and increases infection risk. |
| "If there's no smell, there's no infection" | Many infections including chlamydia, gonorrhoea and early trichomoniasis often have NO symptoms. You cannot rely on smell or appearance alone. |
| "Pain during sex is normal for women" | Persistent pain during intercourse (dyspareunia) is a medical symptom, not a normal part of being a woman. It requires evaluation. |
| "Vaginal steaming cleanses the womb" | No evidence supports this. Steaming can cause serious burns to vaginal walls and disrupt healthy flora, leading to infections. |
| "The hymen determines virginity" | The hymen is a stretchy membrane with natural variation. It can be stretched by many non-sexual activities. It does not prove sexual history. |
| "Public toilets can give you an STI" | Most STI pathogens are fragile and cannot survive on toilet seats. They require close skin-to-skin or fluid contact for transmission. |

---

## The Cervix — The Gatekeeper

*The cervix is the lower, cylindrical part of the uterus that connects the uterine body to the vagina. Approximately 4 cm long and 3 cm in diameter. It is not a separate organ — it's an integral part of the uterus, acting as passageway, protective barrier and producer of critical fluids.*

### Four Critical Functions

**1. Gatekeeper for sperm:** Thick plug-like mucus most of the month; around ovulation becomes thin, clear and stretchy (egg-white) creating a sperm-friendly environment.

**2. Protective barrier:** Remains tightly closed during pregnancy.

**3. Childbirth pathway:** Softens, effaces and dilates to ~10 cm during labour.

**4. Menstrual passage:** Allows menstrual blood to exit.

---

### The Transformation Zone — Why It Matters

The cervix has two cell types: **Glandular cells** (columnar, line the canal, produce mucus — reddish velvet appearance) and **Squamous cells** (flat, protective, cover the ectocervix — smooth pink). Where they meet is the **transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction)** — the most common site for cervical cancer to develop. This is why Pap smears target this area specifically. Its location shifts with age and hormones.

✨ **Cervix Changes You Can Track**

The cervix changes texture and position throughout your menstrual cycle. Around ovulation it becomes **softer, higher and more open** (like pursed lips) to allow sperm entry. After ovulation it becomes **firmer, lower and closed**. Tracking these changes is a valid form of fertility awareness.

---

## Cervical Screening — Kenya Guidelines

| Test | What It Detects | When & How Often |
|------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Pap Smear** | Abnormal cell changes on the cervix that could potentially become cancer | Ages 21–25: every 3 years; Ages 25–65: every 3 years (preferred) or co-test with HPV every 5 years |
| **HPV Test** | High-risk HPV types (especially 16 & 18) that cause cell changes | Ages 26–65: every 5 years (preferred method); can be self-collected |
| **Co-testing** | Both HPV + Pap together | Every 5 years, ages 25–65 |
| **HIV-positive women** | Pap smear every year from age 21 | Annual — HIV increases cervical cancer risk significantly |

🇰🇪 **Kenya Context**

Kenya transitioned to a **single-dose HPV vaccination schedule in November 2025**, making it easier to reach more girls. The HPV vaccine is free of charge at public health facilities for girls aged 10 years. Research by Kenyan doctors — Dr. Nelly Mugo, Dr. Elizabeth Bukusi, Dr. Maricianah Onono and Dr. Betty Njoroge through the KENSHE study (KEMRI/University of Washington) — was instrumental in establishing single-dose efficacy globally.

---

## Uterus, Fallopian Tubes & Ovaries

---

### The Uterus (Womb)

A hollow, pear-shaped muscular organ — the central anatomical landmark of the female internal genitalia. Before pregnancy it is ~7–8 cm long. During pregnancy it expands to the ribcage and can weigh up to 1 kg. After menopause it atrophies and shrinks back down. About 80% of uteri are **"anteverted"** (tilted forward toward the bladder); others are **"retroverted"** (tilted backward) — both are normal variations, not problems.

**Three Layers of the Uterine Wall**

**Perimetrium:** Thin outer serous membrane covering the uterus.

**Myometrium:** The thick middle muscular layer — powerfully contracts during menstruation and labour. Where fibroids grow.

**Endometrium:** The inner mucosal layer with two sublayers — the permanent *basal layer* and the *functional layer* that thickens and sheds monthly.

**Four Parts of the Uterus**

**Fundus:** Broad, curved top above the fallopian tube openings.

**Body (Corpus):** Main central portion where most of the organ is.

**Isthmus:** Narrowed lower neck just above the cervix.

**Cervix:** The lower cylindrical part connecting to the vagina (detailed above).

Held in place by broad, round and uterosacral ligaments.

**Three Key Functions**

**1. Menstruation:** Each month, the endometrium thickens in preparation for potential pregnancy; sheds if no fertilisation occurs.

**2. Implantation & fetal development:** A fertilised egg implants into the nutrient-rich endometrium; the uterus becomes the fetus's home throughout pregnancy.

**3. Labour & delivery:** Myometrial contractions dilate the cervix and push the baby through the birth canal.

---

### The Fallopian Tubes — Where Fertilisation Happens

Two narrow, muscular canals (~11–12 cm long) connecting the ovaries to the uterus. The tubes are *not* directly attached to the ovaries — they have finger-like projections called **fimbriae** that reach out to sweep the egg into the tube at ovulation. The tubes are alive with movement: cilia create a current and muscular walls contract to transport egg, sperm and embryo.

**Four Regions of Each Tube**

**Intramural:** The shortest, narrowest section passing through the uterine wall.

**Isthmus:** Narrow segment next to the uterus.

**Ampulla:** The longest, widest part — most common site of fertilisation. Has folded lining for increased surface area.

**Infundibulum:** The funnel-shaped open end near the ovary, fringed with fimbriae.

**Tubal Conditions**

**Salpingitis/PID:** Infection (usually chlamydia/gonorrhoea) causing inflammation, often with no symptoms. Can scar and block tubes, causing infertility.

**Hydrosalpinx:** Fluid-filled blocked tube — often from prior infection; causes infertility.

**Ectopic Pregnancy:** Fertilised egg implants in the tube instead of the uterus — a **medical emergency**. Symptoms: sudden sharp one-sided pain, vaginal bleeding, shoulder tip pain, dizziness. Requires immediate care.

**Tubal factor infertility:** Accounts for up to one-third of infertility cases.

---

### The Ovaries — Hormonal Architects

Two small, oval-shaped organs (~3.5 × 2 × 1 cm in reproductive years; shrink after menopause) — the female equivalent of the testes. They have two essential roles: producing eggs and secreting hormones.

**Egg Production — A Finite Resource**

You are born with all the eggs you will ever have: ~6–7 million in utero, ~1–2 million at birth, ~300,000 at puberty. Only 300–400 will ever be ovulated. The rest naturally degenerate through **atresia**. You cannot make new eggs. This is why age-related fertility decline is real — both egg quantity and quality decrease over time.

**Hormones the Ovaries Produce**

**Estrogen:** Develops secondary sex characteristics, thickens the uterine lining, maintains bone density, skin health, mood.

**Progesterone:** Prepares the uterine lining for implantation; dominant in the second half of the cycle; maintains early pregnancy.

**Testosterone:** Yes — women produce testosterone in small amounts; plays roles in libido, mood and muscle mass.

**Inhibin:** Regulates FSH production in the pituitary.

⚠️ **Seek Urgent Care If:**

Sudden, severe, one-sided pelvic pain could indicate **ovarian torsion** (twisting of the ovary on its ligaments, cutting off blood supply) or a **ruptured ovarian cyst** — both are medical emergencies. Pain accompanied by fever, nausea/vomiting or faintness requires immediate attention. Heavy bleeding with pain, or bleeding combined with a positive pregnancy test, also warrant urgent evaluation.

---

## The Urethra — Urinary Pathway

*The urethra is a narrow tube (~4 cm long) connecting the urinary bladder to the outside. Its primary job is urine elimination — it is NOT part of the reproductive system. However, because of its close proximity to the vagina and anus, it is deeply connected to pelvic health.*

### Structure: Three Layers

**Mucosal layer (inner):** Lined with transitional epithelium near the bladder, squamous near the opening. Contains folds allowing stretching.

**Spongy layer (submucosa):** Rich in blood vessels and elastic fibres; helps seal the urethra closed when not in use.

**Muscular layer (outer):** Smooth muscle fibres plus the external sphincter (voluntary control).

### Two Sphincters Control Urination

**Internal urethral sphincter:** Involuntary — opens automatically when the bladder is full.

**External urethral sphincter:** Voluntary — you control this to hold urine or let it out. Supported by the pelvic floor muscles.

The sensation "I need to pee" is triggered by **stretch receptors in the bladder wall**, not the urethra, when the bladder is about half full.

---

## UTI — Urinary Tract Infection

A UTI is **not an STI** — it is a completely separate system. Most commonly caused by E. coli from the digestive tract entering the urethra. The short female urethra (~4 cm vs 20 cm in males) is why women are far more prone.

| Symptom | Risk Factor | Prevention |
|---------|------------|-----------|
| Pain or burning during urination (dysuria) | Wiping back to front (brings bacteria forward) | **Always wipe front to back** — single most important hygiene habit |
| Frequent urge to urinate, passing only small amounts | Holding urine for too long | Urinate when you feel the urge; don't hold it |
| Cloudy, dark or bloody urine | Sexual activity ("honeymoon cystitis" — bacteria pushed into urethra during intercourse) | **Urinate after sex** — one of the most effective prevention strategies |
| Strong-smelling urine | Menopause (low oestrogen thins urethral tissues, reducing defences) | Stay hydrated — dilutes urine and flushes bacteria |
| Pelvic pressure or incomplete emptying | Spermicides or diaphragms | Wear breathable cotton underwear; avoid tight synthetics |

🚨 **Seek Urgent Care — Signs the Infection Has Reached the Kidneys**

**Fever, chills or shaking · Nausea or vomiting · Pain in your back or side (flank pain, just below ribs) · Inability to urinate · Visibly bloody urine (red or pink)**

These indicate **pyelonephritis** (kidney infection) — a more serious condition requiring immediate treatment. A simple lower UTI often has NO fever — do not wait for fever to seek care.

---

## Kenya Myth-Busting: Urinary Health

| ❌ Myth | ✅ Truth |
|--------|---------|
| "Drinking less water will reduce the burning" | Burning is caused by inflammation, not water volume. Drinking less concentrates urine, making burning worse. Drinking more helps dilute and flush bacteria. |
| "If I have a UTI, I will always have a fever" | A simple lower UTI (urethritis/cystitis) often causes NO fever. Fever signals the infection has moved up to the kidneys — a more serious condition. You can be very sick with a UTI without early fever. |
| "You can stop antibiotics once the burning stops" | Dangerous. Stopping early leaves the strongest bacteria behind, creating a resistant recurrent infection. Always finish the full prescribed course.

## Barrier Methods

*Only condoms protect against STIs.*

---

### Male Condom

**How to Use Correctly**

- Put it on **before any genital contact** (pre-ejaculatory fluid can contain sperm)
- Pinch the tip to leave space for semen
- Roll down to the base of the erect penis
- After ejaculation, hold the rim and withdraw while still erect
- **New condom for every act of sex**
- Always check the expiry date
- Use **water-based or silicone-based lubricant only** — oil-based products weaken latex and cause breakage
- Available free at public health facilities, inexpensively at pharmacies

**Effectiveness:** 98% perfect use / 85% typical use

**The only method that protects against both pregnancy AND STIs/HIV.**

✅ No hormones; widely available; affordable; different sizes and textures available; can be used *alongside* other methods for dual protection.

❌ Must be used correctly every time; can interrupt spontaneity; some people have latex allergy (non-latex options available — polyurethane or polyisoprene).

*Latex allergy? Non-latex condoms are available — ask your provider or pharmacist.*

---

### Female Condom

A soft polyurethane pouch with flexible rings at each end, worn inside the vagina. **Effectiveness: 79–95%**. It protects against both pregnancy and STIs/HIV — and it is **woman-controlled**, giving women the power to protect themselves without relying on a partner. Can be inserted up to 8 hours before sex. Made of polyurethane — safe for latex allergies and not affected by oil-based lubricants. Requires practice to insert correctly.

---

### Diaphragm & Cervical Cap

A reusable dome-shaped silicone cup inserted into the vagina to cover the cervix before sex — must be used with spermicide. **~88% effective with perfect use**. Must be fitted by a trained provider. Hormone-free and reusable (lasts 1–2 years). May increase UTI risk. Not widely available in Kenya — larger private clinics are most likely to offer fitting.

------------------------------

## Contraception: A Story About Choice

Contraception (family planning) allows you to prevent pregnancy and plan your family. Kenya has a wide range of methods available — from short-term to permanent. The "best" method is the one that works for your body, your lifestyle, your relationship and your future plans. There is no one-size-fits-all.

- **57%** — Married Kenyan women using a modern contraceptive method (KDHS 2022) — up from 32% two decades ago
- **14%** — Unmet need for contraception (women wanting to delay/stop childbearing but not using contraception) — down from 27% in 2003
- **88%** — Kenyan women now delivering in a health facility — a major improvement in maternal safety

💡 **The Golden Rule**

Only **condoms** protect against both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV. If you are at risk of STIs, use condoms even if you are using another method for pregnancy prevention. This is called **dual method use**.

---

## All Methods at a Glance — Comparison Table

| Method | Effectiveness | Duration | Kenya Cost | STI Protection |
|--------|-------------|---------|-----------|---------------|
| **Implant (Implanon/Jadelle)** | >99% | 3–5 years | KSh 300 | ❌ No |
| **Copper IUD** | >99% | 5–12 years | KSh 200 | ❌ No |
| **Hormonal IUS (Mirena)** | >99% | 3–6 years | Higher cost | ❌ No |
| **Injectable (Depo-Provera)** | 94–99% | 3 months | KSh 100 | ❌ No |
| **Combined Pill (COC)** | 91–99% | Daily | KSh 20/cycle | ❌ No |
| **Progestogen-Only Pill (POP/Mini-pill)** | 91–99% | Daily | Pharmacy | ❌ No |
| **Male Condom** | 85–98% | Single use | Free/low cost | ✅ Yes |
| **Female Condom** | 79–95% | Single use | Low/free | ✅ Yes |
| **Fertility Awareness (FAM)** | 76–88% | Ongoing | Free | ❌ No |
| **LAM (Lactational Amenorrhea)** | 98% | Up to 6 months | Free | ❌ No |
| **Female Sterilisation (Tubal ligation)** | >99% | Permanent | Subsidised | ❌ No |
| **Male Sterilisation (Vasectomy)** | >99% | Permanent | Low cost | ❌ No |

---

## Myth-Busting: Contraception in Kenya

| ❌ Myth | ✅ Truth |
|--------|---------|
| "Contraceptives cause infertility" | Modern contraceptives do not cause infertility. For most methods, fertility returns immediately or within a few months after stopping. The only exception is sterilisation, which is intended to be permanent. |
| "If you're breastfeeding, you can't get pregnant" | Only true if ALL three LAM conditions are met: exclusively breastfeeding, baby under 6 months, AND periods have not returned. If any condition is missing, you need additional contraception. |
| "Contraceptives cause cancer" | The combined pill slightly increases breast and cervical cancer risk, but also significantly reduces ovarian, endometrial and colorectal cancer risk. For most women, benefits outweigh risks. Discuss your personal risk with a provider. |
| "Women who use contraceptives are promiscuous" | Women use contraception for many valid reasons: to space children, complete education, protect health, plan families. Contraception is a tool for empowerment, not a moral judgement. |
| "Emergency contraception is the abortion pill" | EC prevents pregnancy by delaying ovulation — it does not work if a woman is already pregnant. The abortion pill (mifepristone) ends an existing pregnancy. They are completely different medications. |
| "Men won't agree to family planning" | Many men in Kenya support family planning when they understand its benefits. Engaging men as partners — through education, counselling and couples' visits — improves outcomes for everyone. |
| "Long-acting methods are not suitable for young women or those who haven't had children" | LARCs like implants and IUDs are safe and recommended for most women, including adolescents and nulliparous women. They are among the most effective methods available and fully reversible. |

# Contraception — Your Complete Guide

## Contraception: A Story About Choice

Contraception (family planning) allows you to prevent pregnancy and plan your family. Kenya has a wide range of methods available — from short-term to permanent. The "best" method is the one that works for your body, your lifestyle, your relationship and your future plans. There is no one-size-fits-all.

- **57%** — Married Kenyan women using a modern contraceptive method (KDHS 2022) — up from 32% two decades ago
- **14%** — Unmet need for contraception (women wanting to delay/stop childbearing but not using contraception) — down from 27% in 2003
- **88%** — Kenyan women now delivering in a health facility — a major improvement in maternal safety

💡 **The Golden Rule**

Only **condoms** protect against both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV. If you are at risk of STIs, use condoms even if you are using another method for pregnancy prevention. This is called **dual method use**.

---

## All Methods at a Glance — Comparison Table

| Method | Effectiveness | Duration | Kenya Cost | STI Protection |
|--------|-------------|---------|-----------|---------------|
| **Implant (Implanon/Jadelle)** | >99% | 3–5 years | KSh 300 | ❌ No |
| **Copper IUD** | >99% | 5–12 years | KSh 200 | ❌ No |
| **Hormonal IUS (Mirena)** | >99% | 3–6 years | Higher cost | ❌ No |
| **Injectable (Depo-Provera)** | 94–99% | 3 months | KSh 100 | ❌ No |
| **Combined Pill (COC)** | 91–99% | Daily | KSh 20/cycle | ❌ No |
| **Progestogen-Only Pill (POP/Mini-pill)** | 91–99% | Daily | Pharmacy | ❌ No |
| **Male Condom** | 85–98% | Single use | Free/low cost | ✅ Yes |
| **Female Condom** | 79–95% | Single use | Low/free | ✅ Yes |
| **Fertility Awareness (FAM)** | 76–88% | Ongoing | Free | ❌ No |
| **LAM (Lactational Amenorrhea)** | 98% | Up to 6 months | Free | ❌ No |
| **Female Sterilisation (Tubal ligation)** | >99% | Permanent | Subsidised | ❌ No |
| **Male Sterilisation (Vasectomy)** | >99% | Permanent | Low cost | ❌ No |

---

## Hormonal Methods — How They Work

*Hormonal methods use synthetic hormones to prevent pregnancy — primarily by stopping ovulation. They come in various forms to suit different lifestyles and needs. None protect against STIs.*

---

### 1. Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill (COC / "The Pill")

Contains estrogen + progestin. Works by:
- **Preventing ovulation** (primary mechanism)
- Thickening cervical mucus (blocks sperm)
- Thinning the uterine lining

**Perfect use:** >99% effective  
**Typical use:** ~91% (up to 7 in 100 users pregnant in first year)

A standard pack has 21 active pills, then a 7-day break with a withdrawal bleed. If started on Day 1 of period: immediate protection. Any other day: use condoms for 7 days.

**✅ Pros:** Makes periods regular, lighter, less painful; reduces risk of ovarian, uterine and colorectal cancers; improves acne; fertility returns immediately after stopping.

**❌ Cons:** Must be taken same time every day; doesn't protect against STIs; some medications (HIV, TB, epilepsy drugs) reduce effectiveness; not suitable for smokers over 35, high blood pressure, or blood clot history.

**🚨 See a doctor if:** Severe leg pain/swelling (possible clot); chest pain or shortness of breath; severe headaches or vision changes; yellowing of skin/eyes; if you missed 2+ pills and had unprotected sex.

---

### 2. Progestogen-Only Pill (POP / Mini-Pill)

Contains only progestogen — works primarily by thickening cervical mucus. Some types (containing desogestrel) also stop ovulation.

**Critical difference:** Must be taken at the *same time every day* — the "missed pill" window is only **3–12 hours** depending on the type (vs 24 hours for the COC). Set a daily alarm.

**Best for:** Women who cannot take estrogen; breastfeeding mothers (safe immediately after birth); women with migraines with aura or high blood pressure.

**✅ Pros:** Safe while breastfeeding; can start immediately after childbirth, abortion or miscarriage; fertility returns immediately after stopping; suitable when estrogen is contraindicated.

**❌ Cons:** Irregular bleeding very common; requires strict timing; some medications interfere with effectiveness.

**If late:** If more than 3 hours late (or 12 hours for desogestrel pills) — follow missed pill instructions on package and use condoms for 2 days.

---

### 3. Contraceptive Injection (Depo-Provera / Sayana Press)

A progestin injection into the muscle (buttock or arm) — given every **3 months** by a healthcare provider. Works primarily by stopping ovulation.

**Effectiveness:** 94–99%  
**Kenya cost:** ~KSh 100 per injection at public facilities

One of the most popular methods in Kenya — private, convenient, only needed 4 times a year.

**✅ Pros:** Highly effective; private; periods often become lighter or stop (benefit for many); safe while breastfeeding.

**❌ Cons:** Requires clinic visit every 3 months; delay in return of fertility after stopping (may take several months to over a year); possible weight gain; irregular bleeding early on.

**Mark your calendar:** If more than 2 weeks late for your next injection, you may need pregnancy testing and backup contraception. Bone density may decrease with very long-term use — reversible after stopping.

---

### 4. Contraceptive Implant (Implanon / Jadelle)

A small, thin, flexible rod (matchstick-sized) inserted under the skin of the upper arm by a trained provider. Releases progestin steadily. Lasts **3–5 years** depending on type.

**Effectiveness: >99%** — one of the most reliable methods available

**"Fit and forget"** — once inserted, you don't have to think about it for years, yet it is fully reversible. Fertility returns quickly after removal. Not visible to others.

**✅ Pros:** >99% effective; long-acting; reversible; discreet; safe for those who cannot use estrogen; LARC (Long-Acting Reversible Contraception).

**❌ Cons:** Irregular bleeding is very common (most common side effect — periods may become lighter, heavier, longer or stop); some HIV/TB/epilepsy medications reduce effectiveness; requires trained provider.

**Kenya cost:** ~KSh 300 for insertion/removal at public facilities like Kiambu Level 5.

---

### 5. Contraceptive Patch & Vaginal Ring

**The Patch**

A small beige sticky patch releasing estrogen + progestin through the skin. Applied weekly for 3 weeks, then 1 patch-free week. **~91% effective with typical use**.

✅ Only need to remember it weekly. ❌ Less effective in women over 90 kg; may be visible; less widely available in Kenya.

Shares the same benefits and risks as the combined pill (including small blood clot risk).

**The Vaginal Ring (NuvaRing)**

A small flexible plastic ring inserted into the vagina for 3 weeks, then removed for 1 week. Releases estrogen + progestin. **~91% typical use, >97% perfect use**.

✅ Monthly convenience; user-controlled; lower systemic side effects for some women. ❌ Requires comfort with self-insertion; not widely available in Kenya.

If ring falls out: rinse with cool water and reinsert within 3 hours to maintain protection.

---

## Long-Acting Reversible Contraception (LARCs)

*LARCs are the most effective contraceptive methods available — and they are fully reversible. They are recommended for most women, including adolescents and women who have not had children. Return to fertility is prompt after removal.*

---

### Copper IUD — Non-Hormonal LARC

A small T-shaped plastic device wrapped in copper wire, inserted into the uterus by a trained provider. Copper is toxic to sperm — impairs their ability to move and fertilise an egg. Also causes a slight change in the uterine lining.

**Effectiveness: >99%** — one of the most reliable methods  
**Duration:** 5–12 years (depending on brand)  
**Kenya cost:** ~KSh 200 for insertion/removal  
**Also the most effective emergency contraception** — if inserted within 5 days of unprotected sex.

**✅ Pros:** >99% effective; hormone-free (great for those who can't or prefer not to use hormones); fertility returns immediately after removal; does not affect natural cycle, mood or weight.

**❌ Cons:** May cause heavier, longer, more painful periods (especially first 3–6 months — usually improves); small risk of expulsion or perforation (rare).

**🚨 See a doctor if:** Can't feel IUD strings; feel hard plastic coming out; severe pelvic pain, fever or unusual discharge (possible infection); positive pregnancy test with IUD in place.

---

### Hormonal IUS (Mirena) — Hormonal LARC

A small T-shaped device releasing **levonorgestrel (progestin) locally** into the uterus. Works by thickening cervical mucus, thinning the uterine lining, and sometimes preventing ovulation.

**Effectiveness: >99%** · **Duration: 3–8 years**

Because the hormone is released directly into the uterus, very little enters the bloodstream — **significantly fewer systemic side effects** than pills or injections.

**Key Advantage — Heavy Periods**

The **IUS is a game-changer for heavy, painful periods**. It dramatically reduces menstrual bleeding — many women have very light periods or no periods at all after the first year. It is also used therapeutically for endometriosis, adenomyosis and fibroids (as part of symptom management).

**❌ Cons:** Irregular bleeding/spotting common in first 3–6 months; requires trained provider; more expensive than copper IUD; less widely available in Kenya.

---

## Barrier Methods

*Only condoms protect against STIs.*

---

### Male Condom

**How to Use Correctly**

- Put it on **before any genital contact** (pre-ejaculatory fluid can contain sperm)
- Pinch the tip to leave space for semen
- Roll down to the base of the erect penis
- After ejaculation, hold the rim and withdraw while still erect
- **New condom for every act of sex**
- Always check the expiry date
- Use **water-based or silicone-based lubricant only** — oil-based products weaken latex and cause breakage
- Available free at public health facilities, inexpensively at pharmacies

**Effectiveness:** 98% perfect use / 85% typical use

**The only method that protects against both pregnancy AND STIs/HIV.**

✅ No hormones; widely available; affordable; different sizes and textures available; can be used *alongside* other methods for dual protection.

❌ Must be used correctly every time; can interrupt spontaneity; some people have latex allergy (non-latex options available — polyurethane or polyisoprene).

*Latex allergy? Non-latex condoms are available — ask your provider or pharmacist.*

---

### Female Condom

A soft polyurethane pouch with flexible rings at each end, worn inside the vagina. **Effectiveness: 79–95%**. It protects against both pregnancy and STIs/HIV — and it is **woman-controlled**, giving women the power to protect themselves without relying on a partner. Can be inserted up to 8 hours before sex. Made of polyurethane — safe for latex allergies and not affected by oil-based lubricants. Requires practice to insert correctly.

---

### Diaphragm & Cervical Cap

A reusable dome-shaped silicone cup inserted into the vagina to cover the cervix before sex — must be used with spermicide. **~88% effective with perfect use**. Must be fitted by a trained provider. Hormone-free and reusable (lasts 1–2 years). May increase UTI risk. Not widely available in Kenya — larger private clinics are most likely to offer fitting.

---

## Natural & Permanent Methods

---

### Fertility Awareness Methods (FAMs)

Track biological signs to identify the fertile window. To avoid pregnancy: abstain or use a barrier method on fertile days. To achieve pregnancy: time sex to coincide with the fertile window.

**Signs tracked:**
- *Cervical mucus* — clear, slippery, egg-white on fertile days
- *BBT* — temperature rise after ovulation (confirms it occurred)
- *Calendar tracking* — for women with very regular cycles
- *OPKs* — for predicting the LH surge

**Effectiveness:** 99% with perfect use; 76–88% typical use. Requires daily dedication and discipline.

**✅ Pros:** No hormones, no medical procedures, no cost; acceptable to all cultures and religions; increases body awareness; can be used to either avoid or achieve pregnancy.

**❌ Cons:** NOT a "lazy" method — requires daily tracking and strict discipline; difficult with irregular cycles; requires abstinence or backup method on fertile days (~half the cycle); does not protect against STIs; less effective than LARCs or hormonal methods with typical use.

**Best for:** Highly motivated, organised couples with regular cycles. Learn from a trained instructor before relying on it. Use condoms as backup during the learning phase.

---

### Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM)

Exclusive breastfeeding suppresses ovulation and can prevent pregnancy — **98% effective when ALL THREE conditions are met:**

1. You are **exclusively breastfeeding** (no supplements, no solid foods, no formula)
2. Your baby is **under 6 months old**
3. Your **periods have not returned**

If any one condition changes, switch to another contraceptive method immediately. Free and supports breastfeeding — but only works with strict adherence to all three criteria.

---

### Permanent Methods — Sterilisation

| Method | What It Involves | Key Facts |
|--------|----------------|----------|
| **Female Sterilisation (Tubal Ligation)** | Surgical procedure (usually laparoscopic/"keyhole") permanently blocking or sealing the fallopian tubes. Can be done immediately after childbirth. Done under anaesthesia. | >99% effective. Permanent. Does NOT affect hormones, sex drive or sexual pleasure. Normal periods continue. Low cost at public hospitals (subsidised). Reversal is difficult, expensive and not always successful — only choose this if 100% certain about no more children. |
| **Male Sterilisation (Vasectomy)** | Simple 15–20 minute procedure under local anaesthetic blocking the vas deferens (tubes carrying sperm). Simpler, safer and cheaper than female sterilisation. | >99% effective. Does NOT affect testosterone, sex drive, erections or ejaculation — semen is produced normally, just without sperm. Takes 3 months/20 ejaculations to clear remaining sperm. Semen test needed to confirm success before stopping other contraception. Underutilised in Kenya due to cultural myths — but safe and highly effective. A powerful act of shared responsibility. |

---

## Emergency Contraception (EC)

*Emergency contraception prevents pregnancy after unprotected sex or contraceptive failure (broken condom, missed pills). It is NOT the abortion pill — it prevents pregnancy from occurring by delaying or inhibiting ovulation. It will NOT work if you are already pregnant. It does NOT protect against STIs.*

| Method | How Long After Sex | Effectiveness & Key Facts |
|--------|------------------|--------------------------|
| **Levonorgestrel pills (Postinor-2)** *Available OTC in Kenya · KSh 200–400* | Within **72 hours** (3 days) — the sooner, the better | Up to 95% effective if taken within 24 hours; ~85% at 48–72 hours. Effectiveness decreases with time. May cause nausea, headache, irregular bleeding. If you vomit within 2 hours, take another dose. |
| **Ulipristal acetate (ellaOne)** *Requires prescription* | Within **120 hours** (5 days) | Remains consistently effective throughout the 5-day window — better than levonorgestrel, especially closer to ovulation. More effective in women with higher body weight. |
| **Copper IUD** *Requires clinic visit* | Within **5 days** | **Most effective EC (>99%)**. Also provides ongoing contraception for 5–12 years. No hormones. May cause heavier periods. Best option if you were considering an IUD anyway. |

💡 **Awareness in Kenya**

A study in Nairobi found that although EC (Postinor-2) is registered in Kenya, it was scarcely known or used. Awareness has grown since, but many women and girls still do not know about EC or where to access it. **It is available over-the-counter at most pharmacies without a prescription (levonorgestrel).** The sooner you act, the more effective it will be — do not wait.

⚠️ **EC and HIV Risk**

Emergency contraception does NOT protect against HIV or other STIs. If you had unprotected sex with a partner whose HIV status you don't know, you may also need **PEP (Post-Exposure Prophylaxis)** — which must be started within **72 hours** of exposure. Go to a hospital immediately and ask about PEP.

---

## Where to Access Contraception in Kenya

| Facility Type | Services Offered | Cost |
|--------------|----------------|------|
| **Level 4, 5 & 6 Hospitals** (Sub-county & County hospitals) | Full range: implants, IUDs, injections, pills, condoms, sterilisation | KSh 20–300 (e.g., Kiambu Level 5) |
| **Level 3 Clinics & Dispensaries** | Pills, injectables, condoms; some offer implants and IUDs | Low cost/subsidised |
| **Comprehensive Care Centres (CCCs)** | Integrated HIV and reproductive health services including safer conception counselling | Free for HIV care components |
| **Private hospitals & clinics** | Full range including fertility treatment and ART where available | Varies — higher than public |
| **Pharmacies** | Pills, condoms, emergency contraception; some offer injectables | KSh 20–400 |
| **Online pharmacies (MyDAWA)** | Pills, condoms, EC and ePrEP — delivered discreetly | Market rates; delivery fees may apply |
| **Mobile outreach clinics** | Many counties offer mobile family planning clinics reaching remote and underserved areas | Low/free |

---

## Myth-Busting: Contraception in Kenya

| ❌ Myth | ✅ Truth |
|--------|---------|
| "Contraceptives cause infertility" | Modern contraceptives do not cause infertility. For most methods, fertility returns immediately or within a few months after stopping. The only exception is sterilisation, which is intended to be permanent. |
| "If you're breastfeeding, you can't get pregnant" | Only true if ALL three LAM conditions are met: exclusively breastfeeding, baby under 6 months, AND periods have not returned. If any condition is missing, you need additional contraception. |
| "Contraceptives cause cancer" | The combined pill slightly increases breast and cervical cancer risk, but also significantly reduces ovarian, endometrial and colorectal cancer risk. For most women, benefits outweigh risks. Discuss your personal risk with a provider. |
| "Women who use contraceptives are promiscuous" | Women use contraception for many valid reasons: to space children, complete education, protect health, plan families. Contraception is a tool for empowerment, not a moral judgement. |
| "Emergency contraception is the abortion pill" | EC prevents pregnancy by delaying ovulation — it does not work if a woman is already pregnant. The abortion pill (mifepristone) ends an existing pregnancy. They are completely different medications. |
| "Men won't agree to family planning" | Many men in Kenya support family planning when they understand its benefits. Engaging men as partners — through education, counselling and couples' visits — improves outcomes for everyone. |
| "Long-acting methods are not suitable for young women or those who haven't had children" | LARCs like implants and IUDs are safe and recommended for most women, including adolescents and nulliparous women. They are among the most effective methods available and fully reversible. |

## Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM)

Exclusive breastfeeding suppresses ovulation and can prevent pregnancy — **98% effective when ALL THREE conditions are met:**

---

### The Three Required Conditions

**1. You are exclusively breastfeeding** — no supplements, no solid foods, no formula

**2. Your baby is under 6 months old**

**3. Your periods have not returned**

---

### Important Limits

If **any one condition changes**, switch to another contraceptive method immediately.

LAM is free and supports breastfeeding — but only works with strict adherence to all three criteria. The moment your baby begins taking any supplement, formula or solid food, or your periods return, or your baby turns 6 months old, LAM is no longer reliable protection.

------------------------------

## Long-Acting Reversible Contraception (LARCs)

*LARCs are the most effective contraceptive methods available — and they are fully reversible. They are recommended for most women, including adolescents and women who have not had children. Return to fertility is prompt after removal.*

---

### Copper IUD — Non-Hormonal LARC

A small T-shaped plastic device wrapped in copper wire, inserted into the uterus by a trained provider. Copper is toxic to sperm — impairs their ability to move and fertilise an egg. Also causes a slight change in the uterine lining.

**Effectiveness: >99%** — one of the most reliable methods  
**Duration:** 5–12 years (depending on brand)  
**Kenya cost:** ~KSh 200 for insertion/removal  
**Also the most effective emergency contraception** — if inserted within 5 days of unprotected sex.

**✅ Pros:** >99% effective; hormone-free (great for those who can't or prefer not to use hormones); fertility returns immediately after removal; does not affect natural cycle, mood or weight.

**❌ Cons:** May cause heavier, longer, more painful periods (especially first 3–6 months — usually improves); small risk of expulsion or perforation (rare).

**🚨 See a doctor if:** Can't feel IUD strings; feel hard plastic coming out; severe pelvic pain, fever or unusual discharge (possible infection); positive pregnancy test with IUD in place.

---

### Hormonal IUS (Mirena) — Hormonal LARC

A small T-shaped device releasing **levonorgestrel (progestin) locally** into the uterus. Works by thickening cervical mucus, thinning the uterine lining, and sometimes preventing ovulation.

**Effectiveness: >99%** · **Duration: 3–8 years**

Because the hormone is released directly into the uterus, very little enters the bloodstream — **significantly fewer systemic side effects** than pills or injections.

**Key Advantage — Heavy Periods**

The **IUS is a game-changer for heavy, painful periods**. It dramatically reduces menstrual bleeding — many women have very light periods or no periods at all after the first year. It is also used therapeutically for endometriosis, adenomyosis and fibroids (as part of symptom management).

**❌ Cons:** Irregular bleeding/spotting common in first 3–6 months; requires trained provider; more expensive than copper IUD; less widely available in Kenya.

------------------------------

topic: "womens-health"

---

## Permanent Methods — Sterilisation

| Method | What It Involves | Key Facts |
|--------|----------------|----------|
| **Female Sterilisation (Tubal Ligation)** | Surgical procedure (usually laparoscopic/"keyhole") permanently blocking or sealing the fallopian tubes. Can be done immediately after childbirth. Done under anaesthesia. | >99% effective. Permanent. Does NOT affect hormones, sex drive or sexual pleasure. Normal periods continue. Low cost at public hospitals (subsidised). Reversal is difficult, expensive and not always successful — only choose this if 100% certain about no more children. |
| **Male Sterilisation (Vasectomy)** | Simple 15–20 minute procedure under local anaesthetic blocking the vas deferens (tubes carrying sperm). Simpler, safer and cheaper than female sterilisation. | >99% effective. Does NOT affect testosterone, sex drive, erections or ejaculation — semen is produced normally, just without sperm. Takes 3 months/20 ejaculations to clear remaining sperm. Semen test needed to confirm success before stopping other contraception. Underutilised in Kenya due to cultural myths — but safe and highly effective. A powerful act of shared responsibility. |

---

### Before You Decide

Sterilisation is intended to be permanent. Reversal is difficult, expensive and not always successful. Only choose sterilisation if you are 100% certain you do not want more children. Both partners should be counselled, and the decision should be made freely and without pressure. If you have any doubt, a long-acting reversible method (LARC) such as an IUD or implant offers similar effectiveness while remaining fully reversible.

## Where to Access Contraception in Kenya

| Facility Type | Services Offered | Cost |
|--------------|----------------|------|
| **Level 4, 5 & 6 Hospitals** (Sub-county & County hospitals) | Full range: implants, IUDs, injections, pills, condoms, sterilisation | KSh 20–300 (e.g., Kiambu Level 5) |
| **Level 3 Clinics & Dispensaries** | Pills, injectables, condoms; some offer implants and IUDs | Low cost/subsidised |
| **Comprehensive Care Centres (CCCs)** | Integrated HIV and reproductive health services including safer conception counselling | Free for HIV care components |
| **Private hospitals & clinics** | Full range including fertility treatment and ART where available | Varies — higher than public |
| **Pharmacies** | Pills, condoms, emergency contraception; some offer injectables | KSh 20–400 |
| **Online pharmacies (MyDAWA)** | Pills, condoms, EC and ePrEP — delivered discreetly | Market rates; delivery fees may apply |
| **Mobile outreach clinics** | Many counties offer mobile family planning clinics reaching remote and underserved areas | Low/free |
