## Introduction: Growing Up, Staying Safe in Kenya

Puberty is a time of change — your body grows, emotions shift and you begin to notice the world differently. For many young people in Kenya, this transition can be confusing, especially without accurate information. At the same time, threats to safety — in schools and communities — are real. Knowledge is your best protection.

**What Is Puberty?**

The time when your body matures from a child to an adult. Usually starts between ages **8–14 for girls** and **9–15 for boys**. These changes are driven by hormones — chemical messengers produced by glands in your body.

**Article 53 — Kenya Constitution**

Every child in Kenya has the right to be protected from abuse, neglect and all forms of violence under **Article 53 of the Constitution** and the **Children Act, 2022**. Puberty does not give anyone permission to touch you without your consent — your body belongs to you at every age.

💡 **Key Point**

Knowledge is your best protection. Understanding your body helps you recognise when something is wrong. Knowing your rights helps you speak up. Understanding consent helps you set boundaries.

---

## Body Changes for Girls

*Everyone develops at their own pace. Your friend may start her period at 10 and you may not start until 14 — both are normal. Comparing yourself to others only causes unnecessary worry.*

| Change | What Happens | When (Typical Age Range) |
|--------|-------------|--------------------------|
| **Breast development (Thelarche)** | Small buds form under the nipple, then breasts grow. Usually the *first visible sign* of puberty. | 8–13 years |
| **Pubic hair growth (Pubarche)** | Hair appears on the vulva, then underarms. Driven by adrenal androgens (adrenarche). | 8–14 years |
| **Growth spurt** | Rapid increase in height — slows significantly after menarche begins. | 9–14 years |
| **First period (Menarche)** | Menstruation begins — usually 2–3 years after breast budding. Cycles may be irregular for the first 1–2 years. | 10–16 years (average 12.5) |
| **Vaginal discharge** | Clear or whitish fluid appears — the vagina cleaning itself. Often 6–12 months before first period. | Typically before menarche |
| **Hips widen** | Body prepares for future childbearing — changes in fat distribution. | Throughout puberty |
| **Body odour** | Sweat glands become more active — especially in armpits. Daily bathing and deodorant help. | Throughout puberty |

⚠️ **Important — When to Seek Evaluation**

- Signs of puberty **before age 8** — should be evaluated for precocious puberty
- **No breast development by age 13** — requires evaluation for delayed puberty
- **No period by age 15** (primary amenorrhea) — requires medical evaluation
- It can take **up to 5 years** for cycles to become regular after menarche

---

## Body Changes for Boys

| Change | What Happens | When |
|--------|-------------|------|
| **Testes & scrotum grow** | Usually the first visible sign of puberty in boys | 9–14 years |
| **Penis grows** | Lengthens and thickens | 10–15 years |
| **Pubic hair grows** | Hair appears at base of penis, then spreads to armpits, face, legs | 9–15 years |
| **Voice deepens** | Voice may "crack and break" as the larynx grows — temporary and normal | 10–15 years |
| **Growth spurt** | Rapid increase in height; shoulders broaden; muscle mass increases | 10–16 years |
| **Wet dreams (nocturnal emissions)** | Ejaculation during sleep — involuntary and completely normal. Not a sign of anything wrong. | 11–16 years |

✨ **Good to Know**

Wet dreams are completely normal. They do not mean you are "bad" or that something is wrong. It is your body's way of releasing excess semen. This is a natural part of male puberty that happens to almost all boys.

---

## Vaginal Discharge: What's Normal?

*One of the first signs of puberty in girls is vaginal discharge — fluid that comes from the vagina. This can be alarming if you don't expect it. It is completely normal and a sign of a healthy vagina doing its job.*

### Normal Discharge

- Clear or white (like egg whites or milk)
- No strong smell (or very mild)
- May stain underwear — slightly acidic, bleaches fabric (use panty liners if it bothers you)
- Changes throughout the menstrual cycle: stretchy and clear around ovulation; thicker and whiter before period

---

### See a Provider If

🚨 Seek care if discharge is:

- **Yellow, green, or grey**
- Has a **strong, foul or fishy smell**
- Accompanied by **itching, burning or swelling** around the vulva
- Causing **pain when urinating**
- Frothy or looks like cottage cheese

A simple swab test gives the diagnosis.

💡 A little discharge is normal — it is the vagina cleaning itself. But if it changes colour, smell or causes discomfort, see a healthcare provider. Poor toilet hygiene is a common cause of irritation in young girls. **Always wipe from front to back** to prevent bacteria from the anus reaching the vagina.

---

## Menstruation: What to Expect

**What Happens During a Period**

- The **uterine lining sheds** because no pregnancy occurred
- Bleeding typically lasts **3–7 days**
- Flow is heaviest in the **first 1–2 days**
- Cycles may be **irregular for the first 1–2 years** — normal
- Average blood loss: **30–80 mL** (about 2–6 tablespoons)

**Common Period Symptoms**

- Cramping in lower belly
- Backache
- Bloating
- Mood changes
- Fatigue

*Mild discomfort is common. Pain that stops you going to school or living your life is NOT normal and deserves medical attention.*

🇰🇪 **Kenya Context — Menstrual Dignity**

A study in Kibera found that while **80% of school-going adolescent girls know menstruation is normal**, many still lack access to clean water and private sanitation facilities at school. This makes managing periods with dignity difficult. If your school lacks facilities, speak to a teacher or parent — **you have a right to learn in dignity**.

---

## Hygiene During Puberty

### For Girls

- Change sanitary pads every **4–6 hours** (more often if flow is heavy)
- Wash the vulva with **water only** — no soap inside
- Wipe **front to back** after using the toilet
- Wear **breathable cotton underwear**
- Dispose of used pads properly — **wrap and bin, don't flush**

---

### For Boys

- Wash the penis gently with water and mild soap
- If uncircumcised, gently pull back foreskin and clean underneath
- Change underwear daily

**For Everyone:**

- Shower or bathe daily, especially after sports
- Use deodorant if body odour bothers you
- Wash hands after using the toilet

---

## Body Autonomy: I Own My Body

*Body autonomy means your body belongs to you. No one else has the right to touch it, use it, or make decisions about it without your permission — at any age, in any situation.*

### 4 Key Principles of Body Autonomy

**1. You are the boss of your body.** No one — not a relative, teacher, friend or stranger — has the right to touch you in ways that make you uncomfortable.

**2. Consent must be freely given.** Saying "yes" because you're scared, pressured or tricked is NOT real consent.

**3. Consent can be withdrawn anytime.** Even if you said yes before, you can change your mind.

**4. You have the right to say "NO."** A simple "No" is enough — you don't need to explain.

---

### Safe Touch vs Unsafe Touch

**Safe Touch:** Feels good, caring, helpful. Characteristics: respectful, not secret, not threatening.

Examples: A parent helping you bathe when young; a doctor examining you with a parent present; a welcome hug; a pat on the back.

**Unsafe Touch:** Feels scary, confusing or painful. Characteristics: secret, forced, makes you feel dirty or scared.

Examples: Anyone touching your private parts; being asked to touch someone else's private parts; kisses that make you uncomfortable; being shown sexual pictures.

✨ **Good to Know — Body Part Names Protect Children**

Teaching children the proper names for body parts (penis, vagina, breasts, bottom) is protective — not shameful. Abusers often target children who do not have words for their body parts, making it harder for the child to report what happened. Naming is a safety tool.

---

## The No-Go-Tell Rule

### Step 1 — NO

Say "No" loudly and clearly. "Stop that!" "I don't like that!" "Don't touch me!" You do not need to be polite — say NO firmly.

### Step 2 — GO

Get away from the situation as quickly as possible. Run to a safe place. Leave immediately — do not wait to see what happens next.

### Step 3 — TELL

Tell a trusted adult until someone helps you. **Keep telling** until someone believes you and takes action. Do not give up.

💡 **Safe Secrets vs Unsafe Secrets**

Safe secrets can be kept (like a surprise birthday party). **Unsafe secrets** that make you feel bad, scared or confused should **never** be kept — tell a trusted adult immediately. An adult who asks a child to keep a secret about touching is always wrong, no matter who they are.

# Puberty & Safety

## Introduction: Growing Up, Staying Safe in Kenya

Puberty is a time of change — your body grows, emotions shift and you begin to notice the world differently. For many young people in Kenya, this transition can be confusing, especially without accurate information. At the same time, threats to safety — in schools and communities — are real. Knowledge is your best protection.

**What Is Puberty?**

The time when your body matures from a child to an adult. Usually starts between ages **8–14 for girls** and **9–15 for boys**. These changes are driven by hormones — chemical messengers produced by glands in your body.

**Article 53 — Kenya Constitution**

Every child in Kenya has the right to be protected from abuse, neglect and all forms of violence under **Article 53 of the Constitution** and the **Children Act, 2022**. Puberty does not give anyone permission to touch you without your consent — your body belongs to you at every age.

💡 **Key Point**

Knowledge is your best protection. Understanding your body helps you recognise when something is wrong. Knowing your rights helps you speak up. Understanding consent helps you set boundaries.

---

## Body Changes for Girls

*Everyone develops at their own pace. Your friend may start her period at 10 and you may not start until 14 — both are normal. Comparing yourself to others only causes unnecessary worry.*

| Change | What Happens | When (Typical Age Range) |
|--------|-------------|--------------------------|
| **Breast development (Thelarche)** | Small buds form under the nipple, then breasts grow. Usually the *first visible sign* of puberty. | 8–13 years |
| **Pubic hair growth (Pubarche)** | Hair appears on the vulva, then underarms. Driven by adrenal androgens (adrenarche). | 8–14 years |
| **Growth spurt** | Rapid increase in height — slows significantly after menarche begins. | 9–14 years |
| **First period (Menarche)** | Menstruation begins — usually 2–3 years after breast budding. Cycles may be irregular for the first 1–2 years. | 10–16 years (average 12.5) |
| **Vaginal discharge** | Clear or whitish fluid appears — the vagina cleaning itself. Often 6–12 months before first period. | Typically before menarche |
| **Hips widen** | Body prepares for future childbearing — changes in fat distribution. | Throughout puberty |
| **Body odour** | Sweat glands become more active — especially in armpits. Daily bathing and deodorant help. | Throughout puberty |

⚠️ **Important — When to Seek Evaluation**

- Signs of puberty **before age 8** — should be evaluated for precocious puberty
- **No breast development by age 13** — requires evaluation for delayed puberty
- **No period by age 15** (primary amenorrhea) — requires medical evaluation
- It can take **up to 5 years** for cycles to become regular after menarche

---

| Change | What Happens | When |
|--------|-------------|------|
| **Testes & scrotum grow** | Usually the first visible sign of puberty in boys | 9–14 years |
| **Penis grows** | Lengthens and thickens | 10–15 years |
| **Pubic hair grows** | Hair appears at base of penis, then spreads to armpits, face, legs | 9–15 years |

## Recognising Abuse

*Child abuse is any act that harms a child's health, survival, development or dignity. Under Kenyan law, children have the right to be protected from all forms of abuse. **Abuse is NEVER the child's fault** — no matter what an abuser says.*

| Type of Abuse | What It Includes | Signs to Watch For |
|--------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| **1. Physical Abuse** | Hitting, beating, shaking, burning or any physical harm inflicted on a child | Unexplained bruises, burns or fractures; fear of going home; flinching when touched |
| **2. Sexual Abuse** | Any sexual act involving a child: touching private parts; making a child touch someone else's private parts; showing pornography; taking sexual photos; penetration (defilement under Kenyan law) | Difficulty walking or sitting; bleeding/pain/discharge from private parts; knowledge of sexual acts beyond their age; regressive behaviours (bedwetting, thumb-sucking) |
| **3. Emotional/Psychological Abuse** | Constant criticism, humiliation, rejection, threats; withholding love; witnessing domestic violence | Withdrawn, anxious or depressed; extreme behaviour (very aggressive or very passive); delayed development |
| **4. Neglect** | Failure to provide basic needs: food, shelter, clothing, medical care, education; abandonment | Constant hunger, poor hygiene, untreated medical needs, frequently absent from school |
| **5. Nutritional Abuse** | Withholding food or failing to provide adequate nutrition. A study at Moi Teaching & Referral Hospital found this was the most common form of abuse seen, affecting 39% of abused children. | Stunted growth, extreme thinness, signs of malnutrition |
| **6. Child Labour & Exploitation** | Forcing a child to work in hazardous conditions; trafficking for labour or sex; **early marriage (child marriage)** | Missing school frequently; signs of exhaustion; adult relationships with an older person who provides gifts |

⚠️ **Kenya Law — Penalties for Defilement (Sex with Child Under 18)**

- Child aged **1–11 years:** Possible **life imprisonment**
- Child aged **12–15 years:** Not less than **20 years imprisonment**
- Child aged **16–17 years:** Not less than **15 years imprisonment**

---

## Reporting Pathways in Kenya

*If you or someone you know has experienced abuse, reporting is essential. Kenya has multiple reporting pathways designed to protect survivors and bring perpetrators to justice. Reporting can feel scary, but you do not have to go through it alone.*

| Where | What They Do | Contact / Note |
|-------|-------------|----------------|
| **Police Station** | Take your statement; issue P3 form for medical examination; connect you to Gender Desk or Child Protection Unit | Ask specifically for the **Gender Police Officer** — specially trained for SGBV/child cases |
| **Any Public Hospital** | Medical examination and treatment; evidence collection (within 72–96 hrs of assault); PEP for HIV (must start within 72 hrs); emergency contraception; counselling | Go even if you are unsure — medical care is critical. If possible, do not bathe or change clothes first (preserves evidence) |
| **Department of Children's Services** | Intervene, provide temporary shelter, assist with legal processes | www.childrenservices.go.ke · Sub-County Children's Officer in your area |
| **Schools** | Head teacher, guidance counsellor or class teacher. Schools have child protection policies and are required to report abuse. | You can ask a trusted teacher to accompany you to report |

**Emergency Contacts**

- **116** — Child Helpline Kenya (Free · 24 hours)
- **1195** — GBV Hotline (Free · 24 hours)
- **112** — Police Emergency (24 hours)

---

### Child Protection Organisations

| Organisation | Contact | Services |
|-------------|---------|---------|
| **ChildLine Kenya** | 116 (24/7, free) | Counselling, referral, rescue |
| **HIAS** | 0798 531053 | Legal aid, psychosocial support |
| **Kituo Cha Sheria** | 0720 806531 | Legal aid |
| **Kenya Red Cross** | 0715 820219 | Tracing, support services |
| **HESED Africa** | 020 2010968 | Support services |
| **Witness Protection Agency** | Via police | Protection until justice is served if you face threats from perpetrators |

---

## What Happens After Reporting

1. **Statement taking** — Tell your story to trained officers
2. **Medical examination** — At hospital (bring P3 form from police)
3. **Evidence collection** — If within 72–96 hours of assault
4. **Protection** — Witness protection available if you face threats
5. **Investigation** — Police gather evidence
6. **Prosecution** — Perpetrator is charged in court
7. **Support** — Counselling and psychosocial support throughout

**If You've Been Sexually Assaulted**

- **Do not bathe or change clothes** if possible — evidence is critical
- Go to a hospital **immediately**
- **PEP for HIV** must be started within 72 hours — do not delay
- Get emergency contraception if relevant
- Report to police — you can be accompanied by a trusted adult

**You are not to blame. Nothing you did caused this.**

💡 **Safe Houses & Rescue Centres**

County governments — such as Kakamega — have established safe houses and rescue centres where survivors can be temporarily hosted for protection against threats from perpetrators. The **Witness Protection Agency** offers protection until justice is served. You do not have to face this alone.

Mons Pubis The fatty, rounded area above the pubic bone, covered with pubic hair after puberty. Provides cushioning during activities and protects the pubic bone. Pubic hair removal is a personal choice, not a medical necessity — shaving or waxing can increase the risk of irritation, ingrown hairs and folliculitis. Labia Majora (Outer Lips) Two fleshy folds from the mons pubis to the perineum containing fatty tissue, sweat and oil glands. Outer surface is pigmented with pubic hair; inner surface is smooth. Labia Minora (Inner Lips) Two thin, hairless folds inside the outer lips — highly variable in appearance. Made of erectile tissue (no fat), they swell and may darken during arousal. Female urethra is only ~4 cm long (vs 20 cm in males) — this short distance explains why women are far more prone to UTIs. You cannot insert a tampon into the urethra — it is far too small. Vaginal Opening & Hymen The entrance to the vaginal canal, surrounded by the hymen — a thin, stretchy membrane that varies enormously between individuals (crescent, ring, fringed, or very small). Skene's Glands (Paraurethral) Two small glands on either side of the lower end of the urethra, sometimes called the \"female prostate\" due to functional similarities. They produce fluid into the urethra during arousal, believed to contribute to lubrication and female ejaculation. Their tiny ducts are vulnerable to ascending bacteria — blockage or infection causes skenitis. 💡 Key Point The vulva does not need special products to be \"clean.\" Warm water and gentle care are all that is required. Less is more. Harsh soaps, douches, vaginal sprays and vaginal steaming cause irritation and disrupt natural balance — there is no evidence any of them benefit health. Vulva Hygiene: Daily Do's & Don'ts ✅ Do - Wash the external vulva once daily with warm water only, or a very mild, fragrance-free pH-balanced intimate cleanser - Wipe from front to back after using the toilet — this prevents E. coli reaching the urethra or vagina - Pat gently dry with a clean soft towel (avoid rubbing) - Wear breathable cotton underwear during the day; avoid wearing underwear to bed - Change out of wet clothing (swimsuits, gym wear) promptly — moisture breeds yeast and bacteria - Change sanitary products regularly as per instructions 🚫 Never - Douche — it disrupts healthy bacteria and increases infection risk - Use scented soaps, bubble baths, sprays or wipes on the vulva - Use scented tampons or pads - Attempt vaginal steaming — no proven benefits, risk of serious burns and flora disruption - Wear tight, non-breathable fabrics for prolonged periods - Flush used pads or tampons — wrap and bin them Common Vulvar Conditions Condition Key Symptoms Action Vulvitis Redness, swelling, itching, burning — caused by irritants, infections or allergies Identify and remove trigger; see provider if persistent Bartholin's Abscess Tender, hot, swollen painful lump near vaginal opening; makes sitting/walking difficult See provider promptly — requires drainage Vulvodynia Chronic, unexplained burning, stinging, rawness or pain lasting ≥3 months with no identifiable cause Requires specialist evaluation — treatable Contact Dermatitis Itching, burning, red rash — allergic or irritant reaction (soaps, detergents, lubricants) Remove the irritant; antihistamines or corticosteroids if needed Genital Warts (HPV) Flesh-coloured, cauliflower-like bumps on vulva or perianal area See provider — treatable; HPV vaccine prevents most cases Herpes Painful, fluid-filled blisters or open sores; tingling or burning before outbreak See provider — antiviral treatment reduces outbreaks Lichen Sclerosus White, thin skin patches; intense itching; may cause scarring — increases vulvar cancer risk Regular follow-up with gynaecologist essential The Vagina — Internal Canal The vagina is a stretchy, self-cleaning fibromuscular canal connecting the cervix to the outside world. It serves menstruation, sexual function, conception and childbirth. It is not the same as the vulva — the vagina is purely internal. The Three Layers of the Vaginal Wall 1. Mucosal Layer (Inner) Similar to skin but without glands. Produces moisture via transudation (fluid seeping through walls). Contains rugae — transverse folds like pleats that allow dramatic stretching during sex and childbirth. Hosts Lactobacillus bacteria that produce lactic acid maintaining protective pH 3.8–4.5. 2. Muscular Layer (Middle) Smooth muscle that contracts and expands. Helps expel discharge and menstrual fluid. Surrounded and supported by the pelvic floor muscles — pelvic floor health directly affects vaginal function. 3. Adventitia Layer (Outer) Connective tissue rich in collagen and elastic fibres. Anchors the vagina to surrounding pelvic structures (bladder, rectum, urethra). Allows expansion and recoil. The slightly acidic discharge that can bleach dark underwear is completely normal — it's the vaginal flora doing their job. 💡 The Vagina is Self-Cleaning The vaginal flora — healthy bacteria naturally living in the vagina — are your first line of defence. They maintain an acidic pH that prevents harmful bacteria and yeast from overgrowing. Douching, scented products and vaginal steaming disrupt this system. The vagina is like the eye — it cleans itself and needs no internal washing. Vaginal Infections — The Three Main Types Infection Cause Key Signs Treatment Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) Most common cause of vaginal discharge Overgrowth of harmful bacteria, decrease in Lactobacilli. Triggered by douching, new/multiple sex partners, no condoms. NOT an STI but sexual activity can trigger it. Thin, grey or white discharge; strong fishy odour (especially after sex); mild itching or burning Prescription antibiotics (metronidazole or clindamycin). Partner does not need treatment for first episode. Yeast Infection (Candidiasis) Candida albicans overgrowth Overgrowth of Candida fungus. Risk factors: antibiotic use (kills healthy bacteria), high oestrogen (pregnancy, HRT), uncontrolled diabetes, weakened immune system (HIV/AIDS) Thick, white, cottage-cheese-like discharge; intense itching; redness and swelling of vulva; burning during urination or sex Over-the-counter antifungal creams or suppositories (if confirmed). See provider if first time, pregnant, or recurrent. Trichomoniasis (\"Trich\") STI — Trichomonas vaginalis parasite Sexually transmitted parasite. Many people have NO symptoms and unknowingly spread it. Both partners must be tested and treated. Frothy, yellow-green discharge with strong odour; itching and redness; pain during urination or sex; lower abdominal discomfort Prescription antibiotics (metronidazole). Both partners must be treated to prevent reinfection. Vaginal Atrophy (GSM) Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause Thinning, drying and inflammation of vaginal walls due to decreased oestrogen — most common during menopause or breastfeeding Vaginal dryness, burning, decreased lubrication, pain during sex, urinary urgency, recurrent UTIs Vaginal moisturizers (first-line), lubricants, low-dose vaginal oestrogen (prescription), ospemifene tablets ⚠️ Critical Warning Vaginal symptoms often overlap — yeast infection, BV and trichomoniasis can all cause itching and discharge but require completely different treatments. Self-diagnosis is unreliable. Do not use over-the-counter antifungal creams if you're not certain it's a yeast infection — using them for BV or trichomoniasis will not work and will delay proper treatment. Kenya Myth-Busting: Vaginal Health ❌ Myth ✅ Truth \"The vagina must be washed inside to stay clean\" The vagina is self-cleaning. Its discharge and healthy bacteria keep it balanced. Internal washing (douching) removes good bacteria and increases infection risk. \"If there's no smell, there's no infection\" Many infections including chlamydia, gonorrhoea and early trichomoniasis often have NO symptoms. You cannot rely on smell or appearance alone. \"Pain during sex is normal for women\" Persistent pain during intercourse (dyspareunia) is a medical symptom, not a normal part of being a woman. It requires evaluation. \"Vaginal steaming cleanses the womb\" No evidence supports this. Steaming can cause serious burns to vaginal walls and disrupt healthy flora, leading to infections. \"The hymen determines virginity\" The hymen is a stretchy membrane with natural variation. It can be stretched by many non-sexual activities. It does not prove sexual history. \"Public toilets can give you an STI\" Most STI pathogens are fragile and cannot survive on toilet seats. They require close skin-to-skin or fluid contact for transmission. The Cervix — The Gatekeeper The cervix is the lower, cylindrical part of the uterus that connects the uterine body to the vagina. Approximately 4 cm long and 3 cm in diameter. It is not a separate organ — it's an integral part of the uterus, acting as passageway, protective barrier and producer of critical fluids. Four Critical Functions 1. Gatekeeper for sperm: Thick plug-like mucus most of the month; around ovulation becomes thin, clear and stretchy (egg-white) creating a sperm-friendly environment. 2. Protective barrier: Remains tightly closed during pregnancy. 3. Childbirth pathway: Softens, effaces and dilates to ~10 cm during labour. 4. Menstrual passage: Allows menstrual blood to exit. The Transformation Zone — Why It Matters The cervix has two cell types: Glandular cells (columnar, line the canal, produce mucus — reddish velvet appearance) and Squamous cells (flat, protective, cover the ectocervix — smooth pink). Where they meet is the transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction) — the most common site for cervical cancer to develop. This is why Pap smears target this area specifically. Its location shifts with age and hormones. ✨ Cervix Changes You Can Track The cervix changes texture and position throughout your menstrual cycle. Around ovulation it becomes softer, higher and more open (like pursed lips) to allow sperm entry. After ovulation it becomes firmer, lower and closed. Tracking these changes is a valid form of fertility awareness. Cervical Screening — Kenya Guidelines Test What It Detects When & How Often Pap Smear Abnormal cell changes on the cervix that could potentially become cancer Ages 21–25: every 3 years; Ages 25–65: every 3 years (preferred) or co-test with HPV every 5 years HPV Test High-risk HPV types (especially 16 & 18) that cause cell changes Ages 26–65: every 5 years (preferred method); can be self-collected Co-testing Both HPV + Pap together Every 5 years, ages 25–65 HIV-positive women Pap smear every year from age 21 Annual — HIV increases cervical cancer risk significantly 🇰🇪 Kenya Context Kenya transitioned to a single-dose HPV vaccination schedule in November 2025, making it easier to reach more girls. The HPV vaccine is free of charge at public health facilities for girls aged 10 years. Research by Kenyan doctors — Dr. Nelly Mugo, Dr. Elizabeth Bukusi, Dr. Maricianah Onono and Dr. Betty Njoroge through the KENSHE study (KEMRI/University of Washington) — was instrumental in establishing single-dose efficacy globally. Uterus, Fallopian Tubes & Ovaries The Uterus (Womb) A hollow, pear-shaped muscular organ — the central anatomical landmark of the female internal genitalia. Before pregnancy it is ~7–8 cm long. During pregnancy it expands to the ribcage and can weigh up to 1 kg. After menopause it atrophies and shrinks back down. About 80% of uteri are \"anteverted\" (tilted forward toward the bladder); others are \"retroverted\" (tilted backward) — both are normal variations, not problems. Three Layers of the Uterine Wall Perimetrium: Thin outer serous membrane covering the uterus. Myometrium: The thick middle muscular layer — powerfully contracts during menstruation and labour. Where fibroids grow. Endometrium: The inner mucosal layer with two sublayers — the permanent basal layer and the functional layer that thickens and sheds monthly. Four Parts of the Uterus Fundus: Broad, curved top above the fallopian tube openings. Body (Corpus): Main central portion where most of the organ is. Isthmus: Narrowed lower neck just above the cervix. Cervix: The lower cylindrical part connecting to the vagina (detailed above). Held in place by broad, round and uterosacral ligaments. Three Key Functions 1. Menstruation: Each month, the endometrium thickens in preparation for potential pregnancy; sheds if no fertilisation occurs. 2. Implantation & fetal development: A fertilised egg implants into the nutrient-rich endometrium; the uterus becomes the fetus's home throughout pregnancy. 3. Labour & delivery: Myometrial contractions dilate the cervix and push the baby through the birth canal. The Fallopian Tubes — Where Fertilisation Happens Two narrow, muscular canals (~11–12 cm long) connecting the ovaries to the uterus. The tubes are not directly attached to the ovaries — they have finger-like projections called fimbriae that reach out to sweep the egg into the tube at ovulation. The tubes are alive with movement: cilia create a current and muscular walls contract to transport egg, sperm and embryo. Four Regions of Each Tube Intramural: The shortest, narrowest section passing through the uterine wall. Isthmus: Narrow segment next to the uterus. Ampulla: The longest, widest part — most common site of fertilisation. Has folded lining for increased surface area. Infundibulum: The funnel-shaped open end near the ovary, fringed with fimbriae. Tubal Conditions Salpingitis/PID: Infection (usually chlamydia/gonorrhoea) causing inflammation, often with no symptoms. Can scar and block tubes, causing infertility. Hydrosalpinx: Fluid-filled blocked tube — often from prior infection; causes infertility. Ectopic Pregnancy: Fertilised egg implants in the tube instead of the uterus — a medical emergency. Symptoms: sudden sharp one-sided pain, vaginal bleeding, shoulder tip pain, dizziness. Requires immediate care. Tubal factor infertility: Accounts for up to one-third of infertility cases. The Ovaries — Hormonal Architects Two small, oval-shaped organs (~3.5 × 2 × 1 cm in reproductive years; shrink after menopause) — the female equivalent of the testes. They have two essential roles: producing eggs and secreting hormones. Egg Production — A Finite Resource You are born with all the eggs you will ever have: ~6–7 million in utero, ~1–2 million at birth, ~300,000 at puberty. Only 300–400 will ever be ovulated. The rest naturally degenerate through atresia. You cannot make new eggs. This is why age-related fertility decline is real — both egg quantity and quality decrease over time. Hormones the Ovaries Produce Estrogen: Develops secondary sex characteristics, thickens the uterine lining, maintains bone density, skin health, mood. Progesterone: Prepares the uterine lining for implantation; dominant in the second half of the cycle; maintains early pregnancy. Testosterone: Yes — women produce testosterone in small amounts; plays roles in libido, mood and muscle mass. Inhibin: Regulates FSH production in the pituitary. ⚠️ Seek Urgent Care If: Sudden, severe, one-sided pelvic pain could indicate ovarian torsion (twisting of the ovary on its ligaments, cutting off blood supply) or a ruptured ovarian cyst — both are medical emergencies. Pain accompanied by fever, nausea/vomiting or faintness requires immediate attention. Heavy bleeding with pain, or bleeding combined with a positive pregnancy test, also warrant urgent evaluation. The Urethra — Urinary Pathway The urethra is a narrow tube (~4 cm long) connecting the urinary bladder to the outside. Its primary job is urine elimination — it is NOT part of the reproductive system. However, because of its close proximity to the vagina and anus, it is deeply connected to pelvic health. Structure: Three Layers Mucosal layer (inner): Lined with transitional epithelium near the bladder, squamous near the opening. Contains folds allowing stretching. Spongy layer (submucosa): Rich in blood vessels and elastic fibres; helps seal the urethra closed when not in use. Muscular layer (outer): Smooth muscle fibres plus the external sphincter (voluntary control). Two Sphincters Control Urination Internal urethral sphincter: Involuntary — opens automatically when the bladder is full. External urethral sphincter: Voluntary — you control this to hold urine or let it out. Supported by the pelvic floor muscles. The sensation \"I need to pee\" is triggered by stretch receptors in the bladder wall, not the urethra, when the bladder is about half full. UTI — Urinary Tract Infection A UTI is not an STI — it is a completely separate system. Most commonly caused by E. coli from the digestive tract entering the urethra. The short female urethra (~4 cm vs 20 cm in males) is why women are far more prone. Symptom Risk Factor Prevention Pain or burning during urination (dysuria) Wiping back to front (brings bacteria forward) Always wipe front to back — single most important hygiene habit Frequent urge to urinate, passing only small amounts Holding urine for too long Urinate when you feel the urge; don't hold it Cloudy, dark or bloody urine Sexual activity (\"honeymoon cystitis\" — bacteria pushed into urethra during intercourse) Urinate after sex — one of the most effective prevention strategies Strong-smelling urine Menopause (low oestrogen thins urethral tissues, reducing defences) Stay hydrated — dilutes urine and flushes bacteria Pelvic pressure or incomplete emptying Spermicides or diaphragms Wear breathable cotton underwear; avoid tight synthetics 🚨 Seek Urgent Care — Signs the Infection Has Reached the Kidneys Fever, chills or shaking · Nausea or vomiting · Pain in your back or side (flank pain, just below ribs) · Inability to urinate · Visibly bloody urine (red or pink) These indicate pyelonephritis (kidney infection) — a more serious condition requiring immediate treatment. A simple lower UTI often has NO fever — do not wait for fever to seek care. Kenya Myth-Busting: Urinary Health ❌ Myth ✅ Truth \"Drinking less water will reduce the burning\" Burning is caused by inflammation, not water volume. Drinking less concentrates urine, making burning worse. Drinking more helps dilute and flush bacteria. \"If I have a UTI, I will always have a fever\" A simple lower UTI (urethritis/cystitis) often causes NO fever. Fever signals the infection has moved up to the kidneys — a more serious condition. You can be very sick with a UTI without early fever. \"You can stop antibiotics once the burning stops\" Dangerous. Stopping early leaves the strongest bacteria behind, creating a resistant recurrent infection. Always finish the full prescribed course.",

Many people use \"vagina\" to mean all of this, but the vagina is internal. The vulva is what you see on the outside. Every vulva is unique in size, shape, colour and symmetry — variation is completely normal and beautiful. Mons Pubis The fatty, rounded area above the pubic bone, covered with pubic hair after puberty. Provides cushioning during activities and protects the pubic bone. Pubic hair removal is a personal choice, not a medical necessity — shaving or waxing can increase the risk of irritation, ingrown hairs and folliculitis. Labia Majora (Outer Lips) Two fleshy folds from the mons pubis to the perineum containing fatty tissue, sweat and oil glands. Outer surface is pigmented with pubic hair; inner surface is smooth. Primary role: protect the more delicate inner structures from friction, injury and pathogens. The female homologue of the scrotum. May shrink slightly after menopause as oestrogen declines. Labia Minora (Inner Lips) Two thin, hairless folds inside the outer lips — highly variable in appearance. Made of erectile tissue (no fat), they swell and may darken during arousal. Densely packed with nerve endings. They split at the top to form the clitoral hood (prepuce) and frenulum; meet at the bottom at the posterior fourchette. Asymmetry between sides is completely normal and common. Clitoris (The Full Structure) Much larger than the visible glans. It is a wishbone-shaped organ with: - Glans (visible tip, ~8,000 nerve endings — more than any other human structure) - Body (extends internally beneath the hood) - Crura/Legs (two wings hugging the urethra and vagina internally) - Vestibular bulbs Its only known purpose is pleasure. Develops from the same embryonic tissue as the penis. Urethral Opening (Meatus) The tiny hole below the clitoris and above the vaginal opening where urine exits. NOT part of the reproductive system. Female urethra is only ~4 cm long (vs 20 cm in males) — this short distance explains why women are far more prone to UTIs. You cannot insert a tampon into the urethra — it is far too small. Urine and menstrual products exit through separate channels. Vaginal Opening & Hymen The entrance to the vaginal canal, surrounded by the hymen — a thin, stretchy membrane that varies enormously between individuals (crescent, ring, fringed, or very small). It can stretch from exercise, tampon use or medical exams. Its presence does NOT indicate sexual history. Some people are born without a hymen. First penetration may or may not cause discomfort or bleeding — both are normal. Bartholin's Glands Two pea-sized glands at the 4 o'clock and 8 o'clock positions near the vaginal opening. Not active until puberty. Produce lubrication during arousal. Usually unnoticed when healthy. Can become blocked forming a painless cyst, or infected forming a painful abscess (swollen, tender lump making sitting/walking difficult — requires drainage by a healthcare provider). Hormones the Ovaries Produce Estrogen: Develops secondary sex characteristics, thickens the uterine lining, maintains bone density, skin health, mood. Progesterone: Prepares the uterine lining for implantation; dominant in the second half of the cycle; maintains early pregnancy. Testosterone: Yes — women produce testosterone in small amounts; plays roles in libido, mood and muscle mass. Inhibin: Regulates FSH production in the pituitary. ⚠️ Seek Urgent Care If: Sudden, severe, one-sided pelvic pain could indicate ovarian torsion (twisting of the ovary on its ligaments, cutting off blood supply) or a ruptured ovarian cyst — both are medical emergencies. Pain accompanied by fever, nausea/vomiting or faintness requires immediate attention. Heavy bleeding with pain, or bleeding combined with a positive pregnancy test, also warrant urgent evaluation. The Urethra — Urinary Pathway The urethra is a narrow tube (~4 cm long) connecting the urinary bladder to the outside. Its primary job is urine elimination — it is NOT part of the reproductive system. However, because of its close proximity to the vagina and anus, it is deeply connected to pelvic health. Structure: Three Layers Mucosal layer (inner): Lined with transitional epithelium near the bladder, squamous near the opening. Contains folds allowing stretching. Spongy layer (submucosa): Rich in blood vessels and elastic fibres; helps seal the urethra closed when not in use. Muscular layer (outer): Smooth muscle fibres plus the external sphincter (voluntary control). Two Sphincters Control Urination Internal urethral sphincter: Involuntary — opens automatically when the bladder is full. External urethral sphincter: Voluntary — you control this to hold urine or let it out. Supported by the pelvic floor muscles. The sensation \"I need to pee\" is triggered by stretch receptors in the bladder wall, not the urethra, when the bladder is about half full. UTI — Urinary Tract Infection A UTI is not an STI — it is a completely separate system. Most commonly caused by E. coli from the digestive tract entering the urethra. The short female urethra (~4 cm vs 20 cm in males) is why women are far more prone. Symptom Risk Factor Prevention Pain or burning during urination (dysuria) Wiping back to front (brings bacteria forward) Always wipe front to back — single most important hygiene habit Frequent urge to urinate, passing only small amounts Holding urine for too long Urinate when you feel the urge; don't hold it Cloudy, dark or bloody urine Sexual activity (\"honeymoon cystitis\" — bacteria pushed into urethra during intercourse) Urinate after sex — one of the most effective prevention strategies Strong-smelling urine Menopause (low oestrogen thins urethral tissues, reducing defences) Stay hydrated — dilutes urine and flushes bacteria Pelvic pressure or incomplete emptying Spermicides or diaphragms Wear breathable cotton underwear; avoid tight synthetics 🚨 Seek Urgent Care — Signs the Infection Has Reached the Kidneys Fever, chills or shaking · Nausea or vomiting · Pain in your back or side (flank pain, just below ribs) · Inability to urinate · Visibly bloody urine (red or pink) These indicate pyelonephritis (kidney infection) — a more serious condition requiring immediate treatment. A simple lower UTI often has NO fever — do not wait for fever to seek care. Kenya Myth-Busting: Urinary Health ❌ Myth ✅ Truth \"Drinking less water will reduce the burning\" Burning is caused by inflammation, not water volume. Drinking less concentrates urine, making burning worse. Drinking more helps dilute and flush bacteria. \"If I have a UTI, I will always have a fever\" A simple lower UTI (urethritis/cystitis) often causes NO fever. Fever signals the infection has moved up to the kidneys — a more serious condition. You can be very sick with a UTI without early fever. \"You can stop antibiotics once the burning stops\" Dangerous. Stopping early leaves the strongest bacteria behind, creating a resistant recurrent infection. Always finish the full prescribed course.",

  "/health-library/womens-health/contraception/contraception": "Contraception — Your Complete Guide Contraception: A Story About Choice Contraception (family planning) allows you to prevent pregnancy and plan your family. Kenya has a wide range of methods available — from short-term to permanent. The \"best\" method is the one that works for your body, your lifestyle, your relationship and your future plans. There is no one-size-fits-all. - 57% — Married Kenyan women using a modern contraceptive method (KDHS 2022) — up from 32% two decades ago - 14% — Unmet need for contraception (women wanting to delay/stop childbearing but not using contraception) — down from 27% in 2003 - 88% — Kenyan women now delivering in a health facility — a major improvement in maternal safety 💡 The Golden Rule Only condoms protect against both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV. If you are at risk of STIs, use condoms even if you are using another method for pregnancy prevention. This is called dual method use. All Methods at a Glance — Comparison Table Method Effectiveness Duration Kenya Cost STI Protection Implant (Implanon/Jadelle) >99% 3–5 years KSh 300 ❌ No Copper IUD >99% 5–12 years KSh 200 ❌ No Hormonal IUS (Mirena) >99% 3–6 years Higher cost ❌ No Injectable (Depo-Provera) 94–99% 3 months KSh 100 ❌ No Combined Pill (COC) 91–99% Daily KSh 20/cycle ❌ No Progestogen-Only Pill (POP/Mini-pill) 91–99% Daily Pharmacy ❌ No Male Condom 85–98% Single use Free/low cost ✅ Yes Female Condom 79–95% Single use Low/free ✅ Yes Fertility Awareness (FAM) 76–88% Ongoing Free ❌ No LAM (Lactational Amenorrhea) 98% Up to 6 months Free ❌ No Female Sterilisation (Tubal ligation) >99% Permanent Subsidised ❌ No Male Sterilisation (Vasectomy) >99% Permanent Low cost ❌ No Hormonal Methods — How They Work Hormonal methods use synthetic hormones to prevent pregnancy — primarily by stopping ovulation. They come in various forms to suit different lifestyles and needs. None protect against STIs. 1. Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill (COC / \"The Pill\") Contains estrogen + progestin. Works by: - Preventing ovulation (primary mechanism) - Thickening cervical mucus (blocks sperm) - Thinning the uterine lining Perfect use: >99% effective Typical use: ~91% (up to 7 in 100 users pregnant in first year) A standard pack has 21 active pills, then a 7-day break with a withdrawal bleed. If started on Day 1 of period: immediate protection. Any other day: use condoms for 7 days. ✅ Pros: Makes periods regular, lighter, less painful; reduces risk of ovarian, uterine and colorectal cancers; improves acne; fertility returns immediately after stopping. ❌ Cons: Must be taken same time every day; doesn't protect against STIs; some medications (HIV, TB, epilepsy drugs) reduce effectiveness; not suitable for smokers over 35, high blood pressure, or blood clot history. 🚨 See a doctor if: Severe leg pain/swelling (possible clot); chest pain or shortness of breath; severe headaches or vision changes; yellowing of skin/eyes; if you missed 2+ pills and had unprotected sex. 2. Progestogen-Only Pill (POP / Mini-Pill) Contains only progestogen — works primarily by thickening cervical mucus. Some types (containing desogestrel) also stop ovulation. Critical difference: Must be taken at the same time every day — the \"missed pill\" window is only 3–12 hours depending on the type (vs 24 hours for the COC). Set a daily alarm. Best for: Women who cannot take estrogen; breastfeeding mothers (safe immediately after birth); women with migraines with aura or high blood pressure. ✅ Pros: Safe while breastfeeding; can start immediately after childbirth, abortion or miscarriage; fertility returns immediately after stopping; suitable when estrogen is contraindicated. ❌ Cons: Irregular bleeding very common; requires strict timing; some medications interfere with effectiveness. If late: If more than 3 hours late (or 12 hours for desogestrel pills) — follow missed pill instructions on package and use condoms for 2 days. 3. Contraceptive Injection (Depo-Provera / Sayana Press) A progestin injection into the muscle (buttock or arm) — given every 3 months by a healthcare provider. Works primarily by stopping ovulation. Effectiveness: 94–99% Kenya cost: ~KSh 100 per injection at public facilities One of the most popular methods in Kenya — private, convenient, only needed 4 times a year. ✅ Pros: Highly effective; private; periods often become lighter or stop (benefit for many); safe while breastfeeding. ❌ Cons: Requires clinic visit every 3 months; delay in return of fertility after stopping (may take several months to over a year); possible weight gain; irregular bleeding early on. Mark your calendar: If more than 2 weeks late for your next injection, you may need pregnancy testing and backup contraception. Bone density may decrease with very long-term use — reversible after stopping. 4. Contraceptive Implant (Implanon / Jadelle) A small, thin, flexible rod (matchstick-sized) inserted under the skin of the upper arm by a trained provider. Releases progestin steadily. Lasts 3–5 years depending on type. Effectiveness: >99% — one of the most reliable methods available \"Fit and forget\" — once inserted, you don't have to think about it for years, yet it is fully reversible. Fertility returns quickly after removal. Not visible to others. ✅ Pros: >99% effective; long-acting; reversible; discreet; safe for those who cannot use estrogen; LARC (Long-Acting Reversible Contraception). ❌ Cons: Irregular bleeding is very common (most common side effect — periods may become lighter, heavier, longer or stop); some HIV/TB/epilepsy medications reduce effectiveness; requires trained provider. Kenya cost: ~KSh 300 for insertion/removal at public facilities like Kiambu Level 5. 5. Contraceptive Patch & Vaginal Ring The Patch A small beige sticky patch releasing estrogen + progestin through the skin. Applied weekly for 3 weeks, then 1 patch-free week. ~91% effective with typical use. ✅ Only need to remember it weekly. ❌ Less effective in women over 90 kg; may be visible; less widely available in Kenya. Shares the same benefits and risks as the combined pill (including small blood clot risk). The Vaginal Ring (NuvaRing) A small flexible plastic ring inserted into the vagina for 3 weeks, then removed for 1 week. Releases estrogen + progestin. ~91% typical use, >97% perfect use. ✅ Monthly convenience; user-controlled; lower systemic side effects for some women. ❌ Requires comfort with self-insertion; not widely available in Kenya. If ring falls out: rinse with cool water and reinsert within 3 hours to maintain protection. Long-Acting Reversible Contraception (LARCs) LARCs are the most effective contraceptive methods available — and they are fully reversible. They are recommended for most women, including adolescents and women who have not had children. Return to fertility is prompt after removal. Copper IUD — Non-Hormonal LARC A small T-shaped plastic device wrapped in copper wire, inserted into the uterus by a trained provider. Copper is toxic to sperm — impairs their ability to move and fertilise an egg. Also causes a slight change in the uterine lining. Effectiveness: >99% — one of the most reliable methods Duration: 5–12 years (depending on brand) Kenya cost: ~KSh 200 for insertion/removal Also the most effective emergency contraception — if inserted within 5 days of unprotected sex. ✅ Pros: >99% effective; hormone-free (great for those who can't or prefer not to use hormones); fertility returns immediately after removal; does not affect natural cycle, mood or weight. ❌ Cons: May cause heavier, longer, more painful periods (especially first 3–6 months — usually improves); small risk of expulsion or perforation (rare). 🚨 See a doctor if: Can't feel IUD strings; feel hard plastic coming out; severe pelvic pain, fever or unusual discharge (possible infection); positive pregnancy test with IUD in place. Hormonal IUS (Mirena) — Hormonal LARC A small T-shaped device releasing levonorgestrel (progestin) locally into the uterus. Works by thickening cervical mucus, thinning the uterine lining, and sometimes preventing ovulation. Effectiveness: >99% · Duration: 3–8 years Because the hormone is released directly into the uterus, very little enters the bloodstream — significantly fewer systemic side effects than pills or injections. Key Advantage — Heavy Periods The IUS is a game-changer for heavy, painful periods. It dramatically reduces menstrual bleeding — many women have very light periods or no periods at all after the first year. It is also used therapeutically for endometriosis, adenomyosis and fibroids (as part of symptom management). ❌ Cons: Irregular bleeding/spotting common in first 3–6 months; requires trained provider; more expensive than copper IUD; less widely available in Kenya. Barrier Methods Only condoms protect against STIs. Male Condom How to Use Correctly - Put it on before any genital contact (pre-ejaculatory fluid can contain sperm) - Pinch the tip to leave space for semen - Roll down to the base of the erect penis - After ejaculation, hold the rim and withdraw while still erect - New condom for every act of sex - Always check the expiry date - Use water-based or silicone-based lubricant only — oil-based products weaken latex and cause breakage - Available free at public health facilities, inexpensively at pharmacies Effectiveness: 98% perfect use / 85% typical use The only method that protects against both pregnancy AND STIs/HIV. ✅ No hormones; widely available; affordable; different sizes and textures available; can be used alongside other methods for dual protection. ❌ Must be used correctly every time; can interrupt spontaneity; some people have latex allergy (non-latex options available — polyurethane or polyisoprene). Latex allergy? Non-latex condoms are available — ask your provider or pharmacist. Female Condom A soft polyurethane pouch with flexible rings at each end, worn inside the vagina. Effectiveness: 79–95%. It protects against both pregnancy and STIs/HIV — and it is woman-controlled, giving women the power to protect themselves without relying on a partner. Can be inserted up to 8 hours before sex. Made of polyurethane — safe for latex allergies and not affected by oil-based lubricants. Requires practice to insert correctly. Diaphragm & Cervical Cap A reusable dome-shaped silicone cup inserted into the vagina to cover the cervix before sex — must be used with spermicide. ~88% effective with perfect use. Must be fitted by a trained provider. Hormone-free and reusable (lasts 1–2 years). May increase UTI risk. Not widely available in Kenya — larger private clinics are most likely to offer fitting. Natural & Permanent Methods Fertility Awareness Methods (FAMs) Track biological signs to identify the fertile window. To avoid pregnancy: abstain or use a barrier method on fertile days. To achieve pregnancy: time sex to coincide with the fertile window. Signs tracked: - Cervical mucus — clear, slippery, egg-white on fertile days - BBT — temperature rise after ovulation (confirms it occurred) - Calendar tracking — for women with very regular cycles - OPKs — for predicting the LH surge Effectiveness: 99% with perfect use; 76–88% typical use. Requires daily dedication and discipline. ✅ Pros: No hormones, no medical procedures, no cost; acceptable to all cultures and religions; increases body awareness; can be used to either avoid or achieve pregnancy. ❌ Cons: NOT a \"lazy\" method — requires daily tracking and strict discipline; difficult with irregular cycles; requires abstinence or backup method on fertile days (~half the cycle); does not protect against STIs; less effective than LARCs or hormonal methods with typical use. Best for: Highly motivated, organised couples with regular cycles. Learn from a trained instructor before relying on it. Use condoms as backup during the learning phase. Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM) Exclusive breastfeeding suppresses ovulation and can prevent pregnancy — 98% effective when ALL THREE conditions are met: 1. You are exclusively breastfeeding (no supplements, no solid foods, no formula) 2. Your baby is under 6 months old 3. Your periods have not returned If any one condition changes, switch to another contraceptive method immediately. Free and supports breastfeeding — but only works with strict adherence to all three criteria. Permanent Methods — Sterilisation Method What It Involves Key Facts Female Sterilisation (Tubal Ligation) Surgical procedure (usually laparoscopic/\"keyhole\") permanently blocking or sealing the fallopian tubes. Can be done immediately after childbirth. Done under anaesthesia. >99% effective. Permanent. Does NOT affect hormones, sex drive or sexual pleasure. Normal periods continue. Low cost at public hospitals (subsidised). Reversal is difficult, expensive and not always successful — only choose this if 100% certain about no more children. Male Sterilisation (Vasectomy) Simple 15–20 minute procedure under local anaesthetic blocking the vas deferens (tubes carrying sperm). Simpler, safer and cheaper than female sterilisation. >99% effective. Does NOT affect testosterone, sex drive, erections or ejaculation — semen is produced normally, just without sperm. Takes 3 months/20 ejaculations to clear remaining sperm. Semen test needed to confirm success before stopping other contraception. Underutilised in Kenya due to cultural myths — but safe and highly effective. A powerful act of shared responsibility. Emergency Contraception (EC) Emergency contraception prevents pregnancy after unprotected sex or contraceptive failure (broken condom, missed pills). It is NOT the abortion pill — it prevents pregnancy from occurring by delaying or inhibiting ovulation. It will NOT work if you are already pregnant. It does NOT protect against STIs. Method How Long After Sex Effectiveness & Key Facts Levonorgestrel pills (Postinor-2) Available OTC in Kenya · KSh 200–400 Within 72 hours (3 days) — the sooner, the better Up to 95% effective if taken within 24 hours; ~85% at 48–72 hours. Effectiveness decreases with time. May cause nausea, headache, irregular bleeding. If you vomit within 2 hours, take another dose. Ulipristal acetate (ellaOne) Requires prescription Within 120 hours (5 days) Remains consistently effective throughout the 5-day window — better than levonorgestrel, especially closer to ovulation. More effective in women with higher body weight. Copper IUD Requires clinic visit Within 5 days Most effective EC (>99%). Also provides ongoing contraception for 5–12 years. No hormones. May cause heavier periods. Best option if you were considering an IUD anyway. 💡 Awareness in Kenya A study in Nairobi found that although EC (Postinor-2) is registered in Kenya, it was scarcely known or used. Awareness has grown since, but many women and girls still do not know about EC or where to access it. It is available over-the-counter at most pharmacies without a prescription (levonorgestrel). The sooner you act, the more effective it will be — do not wait. ⚠️ EC and HIV Risk Emergency contraception does NOT protect against HIV or other STIs. If you had unprotected sex with a partner whose HIV status you don't know, you may also need PEP (Post-Exposure Prophylaxis) — which must be started within 72 hours of exposure. Go to a hospital immediately and ask about PEP. Effectiveness: 94–99% Kenya cost: ~KSh 100 per injection at public facilities One of the most popular methods in Kenya — private, convenient, only needed 4 times a year. ✅ Pros: Highly effective; private; periods often become lighter or stop (benefit for many); safe while breastfeeding. ❌ Cons: Requires clinic visit every 3 months; delay in return of fertility after stopping (may take several months to over a year); possible weight gain; irregular bleeding early on. Mark your calendar: If more than 2 weeks late for your next injection, you may need pregnancy testing and backup contraception. Bone density may decrease with very long-term use — reversible after stopping. 4. Contraceptive Implant (Implanon / Jadelle) A small, thin, flexible rod (matchstick-sized) inserted under the skin of the upper arm by a trained provider. Releases progestin steadily. Lasts 3–5 years depending on type. Effectiveness: >99% — one of the most reliable methods available \"Fit and forget\" — once inserted, you don't have to think about it for years, yet it is fully reversible. Fertility returns quickly after removal. Not visible to others. ✅ Pros: >99% effective; long-acting; reversible; discreet; safe for those who cannot use estrogen; LARC (Long-Acting Reversible Contraception). ❌ Cons: Irregular bleeding is very common (most common side effect — periods may become lighter, heavier, longer or stop); some HIV/TB/epilepsy medications reduce effectiveness; requires trained provider. Kenya cost: ~KSh 300 for insertion/removal at public facilities like Kiambu Level 5. 5. Contraceptive Patch & Vaginal Ring The Patch A small beige sticky patch releasing estrogen + progestin through the skin. Applied weekly for 3 weeks, then 1 patch-free week. ~91% effective with typical use. ✅ Only need to remember it weekly. ❌ Less effective in women over 90 kg; may be visible; less widely available in Kenya. Shares the same benefits and risks as the combined pill (including small blood clot risk). The Vaginal Ring (NuvaRing) A small flexible plastic ring inserted into the vagina for 3 weeks, then removed for 1 week. Releases estrogen + progestin. ~91% typical use, >97% perfect use. ✅ Monthly convenience; user-controlled; lower systemic side effects for some women. ❌ Requires comfort with self-insertion; not widely available in Kenya. If ring falls out: rinse with cool water and reinsert within 3 hours to maintain protection.",
  "/health-library/womens-health/contraception/lactational-amenorrhea-method": "Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM) Exclusive breastfeeding suppresses ovulation and can prevent pregnancy — 98% effective when ALL THREE conditions are met: The Three Required Conditions 1. You are exclusively breastfeeding — no supplements, no solid foods, no formula 2. Your baby is under 6 months old 3. Your periods have not returned Important Limits If any one condition changes, switch to another contraceptive method immediately. LAM is free and supports breastfeeding — but only works with strict adherence to all three criteria. The moment your baby begins taking any supplement, formula or solid food, or your periods return, or your baby turns 6 months old, LAM is no longer reliable protection.",
  "/health-library/womens-health/contraception/long-acting-reversible-contraception": "Long-Acting Reversible Contraception (LARCs) LARCs are the most effective contraceptive methods available — and they are fully reversible. They are recommended for most women, including adolescents and women who have not had children. Return to fertility is prompt after removal. Copper IUD — Non-Hormonal LARC A small T-shaped plastic device wrapped in copper wire, inserted into the uterus by a trained provider. Copper is toxic to sperm — impairs their ability to move and fertilise an egg. Also causes a slight change in the uterine lining. Effectiveness: >99% — one of the most reliable methods Duration: 5–12 years (depending on brand) Kenya cost: ~KSh 200 for insertion/removal Also the most effective emergency contraception — if inserted within 5 days of unprotected sex. ✅ Pros: >99% effective; hormone-free (great for those who can't or prefer not to use hormones); fertility returns immediately after removal; does not affect natural cycle, mood or weight. ❌ Cons: May cause heavier, longer, more painful periods (especially first 3–6 months — usually improves); small risk of expulsion or perforation (rare). 🚨 See a doctor if: Can't feel IUD strings; feel hard plastic coming out; severe pelvic pain, fever or unusual discharge (possible infection); positive pregnancy test with IUD in place. Hormonal IUS (Mirena) — Hormonal LARC A small T-shaped device releasing levonorgestrel (progestin) locally into the uterus. Works by thickening cervical mucus, thinning the uterine lining, and sometimes preventing ovulation. Effectiveness: >99% · Duration: 3–8 years Because the hormone is released directly into the uterus, very little enters the bloodstream — significantly fewer systemic side effects than pills or injections. Key Advantage — Heavy Periods The IUS is a game-changer for heavy, painful periods. It dramatically reduces menstrual bleeding — many women have very light periods or no periods at all after the first year. It is also used therapeutically for endometriosis, adenomyosis and fibroids (as part of symptom management). ❌ Cons: Irregular bleeding/spotting common in first 3–6 months; requires trained provider; more expensive than copper IUD; less widely available in Kenya.",
  "/health-library/womens-health/contraception/permanent-methods-sterilisation": "Permanent Methods — Sterilisation Method What It Involves Key Facts Female Sterilisation (Tubal Ligation) Surgical procedure (usually laparoscopic/\"keyhole\") permanently blocking or sealing the fallopian tubes. Can be done immediately after childbirth. Done under anaesthesia. >99% effective. Permanent. Does NOT affect hormones, sex drive or sexual pleasure. Normal periods continue. Low cost at public hospitals (subsidised). Reversal is difficult, expensive and not always successful — only choose this if 100% certain about no more children. Male Sterilisation (Vasectomy) Simple 15–20 minute procedure under local anaesthetic blocking the vas deferens (tubes carrying sperm). Simpler, safer and cheaper than female sterilisation. >99% effective. Does NOT affect testosterone, sex drive, erections or ejaculation — semen is produced normally, just without sperm. Takes 3 months/20 ejaculations to clear remaining sperm. Semen test needed to confirm success before stopping other contraception. Underutilised in Kenya due to cultural myths — but safe and highly effective. A powerful act of shared responsibility. Before You Decide Sterilisation is intended to be permanent. Reversal is difficult, expensive and not always successful. Only choose sterilisation if you are 100% certain you do not want more children. Both partners should be counselled, and the decision should be made freely and without pressure. If you have any doubt, a long-acting reversible method (LARC) such as an IUD or implant offers similar effectiveness while remaining fully reversible.",
