  "/health-library/womens-health/fertility-infertility/fertility-infertility": "Fertility & Infertility Understanding Fertility & Conception Fertility and contraception are two sides of the same coin. For some, the goal is to achieve pregnancy and build a family. For others, the goal is to prevent pregnancy and plan their lives. Both goals are valid and both require accurate information and access to quality healthcare. In Kenya, your right to reproductive health is protected by Article 43 of the Constitution, which guarantees the right to the highest attainable standard of health, including reproductive health. - 3.1 — Kenya's total fertility rate in 2026 (down from 3.4 a decade ago) - 1 in 6 — couples globally experience infertility at some point - 10–15% — of Kenyan couples unable to have a child The Fertile Window & Ovulation Signs For pregnancy to occur, sperm must meet an egg during the fertile window — the days leading up to and including ovulation. The egg lives only 12–24 hours after release. Sperm can survive inside the female reproductive tract for up to 5 days. This means the fertile window is approximately 6 days long: the 5 days before ovulation plus the day of ovulation itself. Sign What It Looks Like How to Track Cervical mucus changes (Most reliable sign) Clear, slippery, stretchy mucus like raw egg white (\"EWCM\") — the most fertile sign. Earlier in cycle: dry or thick white. After ovulation: thicker, cloudy or absent. Check daily with toilet paper or clean fingers. The egg-white phase = peak fertility window. Basal body temperature (BBT) Temperature rises slightly 0.3–0.6°C after ovulation due to progesterone. Stays elevated throughout the luteal phase until next period. Confirms ovulation has occurred — does not predict it. Take temperature every morning before getting out of bed with a BBT thermometer. Track on a chart or app. Ovulation pain (Mittelschmerz) Mild twinge or cramp on one side of the lower abdomen — lasts minutes to a few hours. The side alternates each month. Note in diary or app. Not all women feel this and its absence does not mean no ovulation. Ovulation predictor kits (OPKs) Detect the LH surge that happens 24–36 hours before ovulation — predicts your most fertile days before the egg is released. Available at pharmacies. Urine test similar to a pregnancy test. Begin testing a few days before your expected ovulation. 🇰🇪 Kenya Research — Fertility Awareness in HIV-Serodifferent Couples A study in Thika, Kenya found that among women in HIV-serodifferent couples using fertility awareness methods, reporting \"sticky\" cervical mucus and a positive OPK were significantly associated with having condomless sex during peak fertility days. This confirms that FAMs can be effective tools for couples trying to conceive while managing HIV risk. Fertility Across Life Stages Age Group Fertility Status & Monthly Chance Key Considerations Teens (15–19) Highly fertile, but cycles may be irregular for first 1–2 years after menarche High risk of unplanned pregnancy; need for contraception education and access 20s Peak fertility years — monthly chance of pregnancy 20–25% Best time for childbearing biologically. Egg quality and quantity are at their peak. Early 30s Fertility begins gradual decline — monthly chance 15–20% Decline is slow. Most women in their early 30s conceive without difficulty. Late 30s (35–39) More noticeable decline — monthly chance 10–15% Increased risk of miscarriage and chromosomal abnormalities (egg quality declines). Seek help after 6 months of trying. 40–44 Low fertility — monthly chance &lt;5% Many women in this age group require fertility assistance. Seek help immediately — do not wait. 45+ Very low — natural conception rare Donor eggs often needed for pregnancy. IVF success rates drop significantly with own eggs. 💡 When to Seek Fertility Help - Under 35: After 1 year of regular, unprotected sex without conceiving. - Ages 35–40: After 6 months of regular, unprotected sex without conceiving. - Over 40: Immediately — do not wait. Both partners should be evaluated. Infertility affects men and women equally — about one-third of cases involve female factors, one-third male factors, and one-third both or unexplained. Infertility — Causes & The Diagnostic Journey Infertility is defined as the inability to conceive after 12 months of regular, unprotected sex (6 months if over 35). It is a disease of the reproductive system — deserving the same compassion and evidence-based care as any other health issue. In Kenya, studies suggest 10–15% of couples are unable to have a child. Male factor contributes to 20–70% of infertility cases globally — in Kenya, it's estimated that in 60% of couples struggling to conceive, the problem lies wholly or partly with the male partner. Female Factor Infertility — Main Causes Category Specific Causes Notes Ovulation Disorders PCOS (most common); hypothalamic dysfunction (stress, low body weight, excessive exercise); Premature Ovarian Insufficiency (&lt;40); thyroid disorders; high prolactin Problems with ovulation are a leading cause of female infertility — often hormonal and treatable Tubal Infertility Damage or blockage from PID (untreated STIs — chlamydia, gonorrhoea); previous abdominal or pelvic surgery; prior ectopic pregnancy; tubal ligation (intentional) Accounts for up to one-third of female infertility cases. Often no symptoms — silent damage from untreated STIs. Uterine/Cervical Causes Fibroids (interfere with implantation); endometriosis (inflammation, scarring); uterine polyps or adhesions (Asherman's syndrome); congenital structural abnormalities (bicornuate uterus, uterine didelphys) Many uterine causes are treatable — surgery can often restore fertility Male Factor Infertility — Main Causes Male infertility most often relates to problems with sperm: low count (oligospermia), poor movement (poor motility), or abnormal shape (poor morphology). Category Causes Pre-testicular (Hormonal) Issues with hypothalamus or pituitary failing to signal testicles correctly — hormone imbalances, certain medications, tumours Testicular (Sperm production) Varicocele (enlarged scrotal veins, overheating testicles — seen in ~20% of infertile men); genetic defects (Klinefelter syndrome); infections (mumps after puberty, STIs causing scarring); undescended testicles in childhood; cancer treatment (chemotherapy, radiation) Post-testicular (Sperm delivery) Blocked vas deferens (infection, surgery, vasectomy); ejaculatory dysfunction (retrograde ejaculation); azoospermia (no sperm in semen — if production problem vs blockage determines treatability) ✨ Do NOT Let Anyone Tell You \"You Are the Problem\" Without Testing In Kenya, the burden of infertility has been unfairly placed on women. A simple semen analysis is the first and most important test for a man — painless, non-invasive and inexpensive. It should always be done alongside female investigations. In many cases, male infertility is treatable with simple lifestyle changes, medications or minor surgery. Lifestyle Risk Factors Affecting Both Partners Modifiable Risk Factors - Age — female fertility declines significantly after 35; male declines gradually - Smoking — harms sperm quality and accelerates egg loss - Excess alcohol — impairs sperm production and ovulation - Recreational drugs (cannabis, cocaine) — affect fertility in both sexes - Weight — significantly underweight or overweight disrupts ovulation and sperm quality - Stress — interferes with hormones regulating reproduction - Environmental toxins — pesticides, lead and industrial chemicals Male-Specific Tips - Avoid tight underwear — increases scrotal temperature, temporarily impairing sperm production - Take breaks from prolonged sitting (long-distance driving, desk work) — same reason - Avoid hot baths and saunas frequently - Even small changes help — switching from tight briefs to loose boxers can improve sperm quality over time Sperm production takes ~74 days — lifestyle changes take time to show results. Diagnostic Tests Test For Whom What It Shows Semen analysis Male partner — always done first Sperm count (normal: >15M/mL), motility, morphology, volume. If abnormal, repeat — sperm quality fluctuates. Ovulation testing Female — Day 21 progesterone blood test Confirms whether ovulation occurred in that cycle AMH (Anti-Müllerian Hormone) Female — any cycle day Estimates ovarian reserve (egg quantity remaining). Low AMH = reduced reserve. Does not perfectly predict pregnancy. Day-3 FSH & estradiol Female — day 3 of cycle Elevated FSH suggests declining ovarian reserve — pituitary working harder to stimulate ovaries HSG (Hysterosalpingography) Female — X-ray with dye Checks if fallopian tubes are open and uterine cavity is normal shape. Key fertility test. Pelvic ultrasound Female Examines uterus, ovaries; antral follicle count (indicator of ovarian reserve); checks for fibroids, polyps, cysts Hysteroscopy Female Camera directly visualises inside the uterus — finds and treats polyps, fibroids, adhesions STI screening Both partners Chlamydia and gonorrhoea — untreated STIs cause tubal damage and infertility Genetic testing Both — if suspected genetic cause Very low/zero sperm count, family history of genetic conditions, recurrent miscarriage Fertility Treatment Options 1. Lifestyle Changes & Timed Intercourse For some couples, simple changes — quitting smoking, reaching a healthy weight, reducing alcohol, managing stress, and timing sex to the fertile window using OPKs or FAMs — are all that is needed. Never underestimate the power of lifestyle. This is always the first step. 2. Medical Treatments Medication What It Does For Whom Clomifene citrate Stimulates ovulation — the first-line drug for women who don't ovulate regularly PCOS and other ovulatory disorders; taken days 2–6 of cycle Letrozole Also stimulates ovulation — increasingly preferred over clomifene in PCOS May have better ovulation and pregnancy rates in PCOS than clomifene; lower multiple pregnancy risk Metformin Improves insulin resistance, encourages ovulation in PCOS PCOS with insulin resistance — often combined with clomifene. NOT a weight loss drug. Injectable gonadotrophins (FSH/LH) Directly stimulate follicle development in the ovaries When oral drugs fail — requires close monitoring; higher multiple pregnancy risk Antibiotics Treat underlying infections affecting fertility in either partner If STI or reproductive tract infection identified on screening ⚠️ About Fertility Drugs Fertility drugs can have side effects including hot flashes, mood swings and — with injectable gonadotrophins — an increased risk of multiple pregnancy (twins, triplets). Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is a risk with injectable medications. Always take them under close medical supervision with ultrasound monitoring. 3. Surgical Treatments Procedure What It Does Notes Myomectomy Surgical removal of fibroids, preserving the uterus and fertility Fibroids can regrow — discuss timing relative to fertility plans Polypectomy (hysteroscopic) Removal of endometrial polyps that may interfere with implantation Simple procedure — day case; often dramatically improves IVF outcomes Laparoscopic endometriosis treatment Excision of endometriosis lesions; drainage of endometriomas May improve natural conception and IVF success in selected cases Laparoscopic ovarian drilling (LOD) Minor procedure reducing androgen-producing tissue in ovaries to restore ovulation in PCOS Option when medications fail; lower multiple pregnancy risk than gonadotrophins Varicocelectomy (male) Surgical repair of varicocele — can improve sperm quality Varicocele found in ~20% of infertile men; surgery improves counts in many Vasectomy reversal Restores sperm to the semen after vasectomy 75–90% success rate in restoring sperm; pregnancy rates depend on time since vasectomy and partner age 4. Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) Procedure How It Works Success Rate & Notes IUI — Intrauterine Insemination \"Washed\" and concentrated sperm placed directly into the uterus around ovulation. Often combined with ovulation-stimulating drugs. Less invasive than IVF. ~7–8% pregnancy rate per cycle. Useful for: mild male factor infertility, cervical mucus problems, unexplained infertility, donor sperm use. IVF — In Vitro Fertilisation Eggs retrieved from ovaries and fertilised with sperm in a laboratory. Resulting embryo(s) transferred back into the uterus. Previously known as \"test tube baby.\" Success rates vary by age: ~40% per cycle under 35; drops significantly after 40. Used for: blocked tubes, severe male factor, endometriosis, unexplained infertility. ICSI — Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection A single healthy sperm injected directly into an egg under a microscope. Sperm can even be surgically retrieved from the testicle (TESA/PESA) if not in semen. ~20–30% pregnancy rate per cycle. A game-changer for severe male factor infertility — even men with very few or no sperm in semen may father children. Donor Insemination (DI) Using carefully screened donor sperm to inseminate the woman Option if male partner has no sperm and the condition is untreatable. Legal in Kenya under the new ART Act. Egg/Embryo Donation Using donor eggs (fertilised with partner's or donor sperm) for women whose own eggs cannot be used Option for women with premature ovarian insufficiency, very poor egg quality, or genetic conditions. Now regulated under the ART Act. Fertility Preservation Egg or sperm freezing for those facing medical treatments (chemotherapy, radiation) that could affect fertility, or for those wishing to delay childbearing Egg freezing is most effective under age 35. Now legally recognised in Kenya. Kenya's Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) Act, 2022 In November 2025, the National Assembly passed the Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) Bill, 2022 — a landmark law providing for the first time a comprehensive legal and regulatory framework for fertility care in Kenya. This places Kenya among a handful of African nations with such a forward-thinking framework. Provision What It Means for Kenyans Legalises and regulates fertility treatment IVF, IUI, gamete (egg/sperm) donation, embryo donation and surrogacy are now legally recognised and will be regulated for ethical, safe practice Establishes an ART Committee Under the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Council (KMPDC) — will license clinics, maintain a confidential national register of donors, embryos and children conceived through ART Eligibility criteria Intended parents: Kenyan citizens aged 25–55 years. Surrogate mothers: Kenyan citizens aged 25–45 years, must have borne at least one child and pass medical and psychological assessments. Prohibits commercial surrogacy Only altruistic surrogacy is permitted — surrogates can receive medical expenses but no payment, preventing exploitation Criminalises unethical practices Human cloning, sale of gametes/embryos and sex selection are banned — penalties up to KSh 10 million fine or 10 years imprisonment Parental leave provisions Surrogates: 3 months' leave after birth. Intended mothers and fathers receive maternity and paternity leave respectively. ⚠️ Current Status The law is awaiting Senate concurrence and Presidential assent to become fully operational. Once enacted, it will transform fertility care in Kenya — providing legal clarity, ethical standards and protection for all parties involved in fertility treatment. Safer Conception — Special Considerations for HIV Kenya has a significant HIV burden, and many couples include one HIV-positive and one HIV-negative partner (serodifferent couples). These couples face a unique challenge: wanting to achieve pregnancy while minimising HIV transmission risk to the negative partner and the baby. Modern strategies make this achievable. Strategy How It Works Key Facts Treatment as Prevention (TasP) HIV-positive partner takes antiretrovirals consistently to achieve viral suppression When viral load is undetectable, risk of transmission is effectively zero — U=U (Undetectable = Untransmissible) PrEP (Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis) HIV-negative partner takes daily pill OR injectable lenacapavir (Sunlenca) every 6 months to prevent HIV acquisition Daily oral PrEP reduces risk by up to 95%. Injectable lenacapavir (twice yearly) is now available as an alternative. Timed condomless sex Using fertility awareness methods to identify the fertile window — having condomless sex only during those peak days A Thika study confirmed FAM-based timing can align condomless sex with peak fertility. Antiretroviral-based strategies remain essential alongside this. Self-insemination Partner's sperm used for at-home insemination during the fertile window — avoids HIV exposure entirely Can be done without clinical assistance; avoids any sexual transmission risk Sperm washing + IVF/IUI Sperm is \"washed\" to eliminate the virus, then used for IVF or IUI Available at specialised fertility clinics; expensive but highly effective at eliminating risk 💡 ePrEP — Innovative Access in Kenya An innovative ePrEP model is making HIV prevention more accessible in Kenya. Through partnerships with online pharmacies like MyDAWA, individuals can access PrEP and other prevention tools privately and conveniently. As Dr. Daniel Were of Jhpiego explains, bundling emergency contraception with HIV preventive tools ensures holistic care is addressed. Coping with Infertility — Emotional Support Strategies That Help 1. Talk to each other — infertility can strain a relationship; keep communication open and honest 2. Seek counselling — a counsellor specialising in infertility provides a safe space to process grief, anger and frustration 3. Find support groups — connecting with others on the same journey is validating; online communities and forums can provide support where formal groups are limited 4. Set boundaries — it is okay to protect your mental health by stepping back from baby showers or events that feel too painful 5. Take breaks from treatment — the emotional and financial toll can be overwhelming; it is okay to pause and focus on yourselves What to Remember - Infertility is a medical condition — not a punishment, not a curse, not your fault - Your emotional health matters as much as your physical health - Stress does contribute to hormonal disruption — prioritising mental health is medically important, not just a luxury - Even with unexplained infertility, many couples go on to conceive — either naturally over time or with less intensive treatments - You are not alone — millions of couples worldwide are on this same journey Seeking support is a sign of strength, not weakness. You deserve care for both your body and your heart. Myth-Busting: Fertility in Kenya ❌ Myth ✅ Truth \"Infertility is always the woman's problem\" Infertility affects men and women equally. In Kenya, up to 60% of couples struggling to conceive have a problem wholly or partly with the male partner. Both partners must be evaluated. \"If you haven't conceived after a few months, something is wrong\" Even for young, healthy couples, the chance of conceiving in any given month is only 20–25%. It can take up to a year of trying before pregnancy occurs — this is normal. Seek help after 1 year (6 months if over 35). \"IVF always works\" IVF success rates vary significantly with age: about 40% per cycle under 35, dropping to under 10% per cycle over 42 with own eggs. It often takes multiple cycles. Have realistic expectations. \"Traditional herbs can boost fertility\" No herbal remedy has been scientifically proven to restore fertility. Relying on herbs can delay diagnosis and proper treatment. Some herbs can interfere with medications. Always tell your provider about anything you are taking. \"You can tell you're fertile just by how regular your periods are\" Regular periods do not guarantee ovulation or fertility. Many women have regular cycles but do not ovulate every month (anovulation). The only way to confirm ovulation is through monitoring.",

Both partners must be evaluated. \"If you haven't conceived after a few months, something is wrong\" Even for young, healthy couples, the chance of conceiving in any given month is only 20–25%.   "/health-library/womens-health/fertility-infertility/understanding-fertility-and-conception": "Understanding Fertility & Conception Fertility and contraception are two sides of the same coin. For some, the goal is to achieve pregnancy and build a family. For others, the goal is to prevent pregnancy and plan their lives. Both goals are valid and both require accurate information and access to quality healthcare. In Kenya, your right to reproductive health is protected by Article 43 of the Constitution, which guarantees the right to the highest attainable standard of health, including reproductive health. - 3.1 — Kenya's total fertility rate in 2026 (down from 3.4 a decade ago) - 1 in 6 — couples globally experience infertility at some point - 10–15% — of Kenyan couples unable to have a child The Fertile Window & Ovulation Signs For pregnancy to occur, sperm must meet an egg during the fertile window — the days leading up to and including ovulation. The egg lives only 12–24 hours after release. Sperm can survive inside the female reproductive tract for up to 5 days. This means the fertile window is approximately 6 days long: the 5 days before ovulation plus the day of ovulation itself. Sign What It Looks Like How to Track Cervical mucus changes (Most reliable sign) Clear, slippery, stretchy mucus like raw egg white (\"EWCM\") — the most fertile sign. Earlier in cycle: dry or thick white. After ovulation: thicker, cloudy or absent. Check daily with toilet paper or clean fingers. The egg-white phase = peak fertility window. Basal body temperature (BBT) Temperature rises slightly 0.3–0.6°C after ovulation due to progesterone. Stays elevated throughout the luteal phase until next period. Confirms ovulation has occurred — does not predict it. Take temperature every morning before getting out of bed with a BBT thermometer. Track on a chart or app. Ovulation pain (Mittelschmerz) Mild twinge or cramp on one side of the lower abdomen — lasts minutes to a few hours. The side alternates each month. Note in diary or app. Not all women feel this and its absence does not mean no ovulation. Ovulation predictor kits (OPKs) Detect the LH surge that happens 24–36 hours before ovulation — predicts your most fertile days before the egg is released. Available at pharmacies. Urine test similar to a pregnancy test. Begin testing a few days before your expected ovulation. 🇰🇪 Kenya Research — Fertility Awareness in HIV-Serodifferent Couples A study in Thika, Kenya found that among women in HIV-serodifferent couples using fertility awareness methods, reporting \"sticky\" cervical mucus and a positive OPK were significantly associated with having condomless sex during peak fertility days. This confirms that FAMs can be effective tools for couples trying to conceive while managing HIV risk.   "/health-library/womens-health/gynaecological-conditions/gynaecological-conditions": "Gynaecological Conditions & Cancers Introduction: What Are Gynaecological Conditions? Gynaecological conditions affect the uterus, ovaries, fallopian tubes, cervix, vagina and vulva. They range from benign growths and hormonal disorders to infections and cancers. Many share overlapping symptoms — which is why proper diagnosis matters. Self-diagnosing based on a friend's experience can lead to years of unnecessary suffering. - 190M women worldwide with endometriosis - 70–80% of women develop fibroids by age 50 - 5,845 cervical cancer cases per year in Kenya Endometriosis Endometriosis is a condition where tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus — on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, bowel, bladder, and other pelvic structures. This misplaced tissue responds to hormonal cycles: thickening, breaking down and bleeding with each period, but with no way to exit the body. This causes inflammation, scarring, adhesions and chronic pain. It is one of the leading causes of infertility. Key Symptoms of Endometriosis - Severe, debilitating period pain (dysmenorrhea) that OTC medication doesn't help - Chronic pelvic pain even when not on your period - Pain during or after sex (deep dyspareunia) - Heavy menstrual bleeding or bleeding between periods - Pain when urinating or having a bowel movement, especially during your period - Fatigue - Difficulty conceiving (infertility) - Mood disorders and anxiety - If in the chest: shortness of breath, coughing blood Diagnosis & The 4–12 Year Delay The average time to diagnose endometriosis is 4–12 years — because symptoms are often dismissed as \"normal period pain.\" Investigations: - Pelvic exam — may feel cysts or scars behind the uterus - Transvaginal ultrasound — can identify endometriomas (\"chocolate cysts\") on ovaries - MRI — detailed images of deeper lesions - Laparoscopy — minimally invasive surgery; the gold standard for definitive diagnosis. Allows direct visualisation and biopsy of lesions. Treatment Options for Endometriosis There is no cure for endometriosis, but treatment can manage symptoms. Treatment What It Does Notes NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) Reduce mild pain by lowering prostaglandins First-line for pain management; often insufficient alone for severe endometriosis Combined contraceptive pill Suppresses the hormonal cycle that drives growth and bleeding of lesions Must be stopped if trying to conceive — discuss timing with provider Mirena IUD (hormonal coil) Progestin locally thins the uterine lining; reduces pain and bleeding Also provides contraception; fertility returns upon removal GnRH agonists Temporarily induce menopause by suppressing estrogen, shrinking lesions Usually short-term (max 6 months) — can cause bone loss and menopausal symptoms Laparoscopic excision Surgical removal (\"cutting out\") of lesions — significant pain relief and improved fertility Can be combined with treatment of endometriomas; may need repeat procedures IVF / Fertility treatment Assisted fertility methods if endometriosis affects conception Discuss timing carefully — surgery may improve IVF outcomes in some cases 🇰🇪 In Memory: Njambi Koikai In Kenya, we remember Njambi Koikai — an endometriosis warrior whose courage transformed pain into powerful advocacy. She spoke boldly about living with the condition, demanding better awareness and better healthcare for women whose pain is too often dismissed. As we honour her, we recommit to listening to women, believing their pain and pushing for better care for every endometriosis warrior. Uterine Fibroids (Leiomyomas) Fibroids are benign (non-cancerous) growths of smooth muscle and fibrous tissue that develop in or on the uterus. They range from tiny seedlings to large masses distorting the uterus. Around 2 in 3 women develop at least one fibroid. Many have no symptoms and don't know they have them — diagnosed by chance during a routine scan. 4 Types by Location - Submucosal: Grow just under the uterine lining, bulging into the cavity. Most likely to cause heavy bleeding and infertility. - Intramural: Grow within the muscular wall of the uterus — the most common type. - Subserosal: Grow on the outside of the uterus, projecting into the pelvis. Can cause pressure symptoms. - Pedunculated: Subserosal or submucosal fibroids on a stalk — can occasionally twist (torsion), causing acute pain. Key Symptoms of Uterine Fibroids (only 1 in 3 women have symptoms) - Heavy, prolonged menstrual bleeding — sometimes with large clots - Pelvic pressure and pain (feeling of fullness or heaviness) - Frequent urination (pressure on bladder) - Constipation (pressure on bowel) - Backache or leg pain - Pain during sex - Infertility or pregnancy complications (depending on location) Diagnosis Methods Test What It Shows Pelvic exam May reveal enlarged, irregularly shaped uterus Ultrasound (transvaginal or abdominal) Primary imaging tool — identifies fibroids, maps location, measures size Hysteroscopy Camera through vagina and cervix into womb — best for submucosal fibroids. Takes 10–15 minutes; can feel like period cramping. Laparoscopy Camera through small abdominal incision; done under general anaesthesia — examines outside of uterus MRI Used for complex cases or detailed pre-surgical mapping Treatment Options for Uterine Fibroids — Tailored to Your Goals Treatment What It Does Best For Watchful waiting Fibroids often shrink after menopause; monitor if asymptomatic No symptoms or mild symptoms near menopause Mirena IUS Releases progestin locally — thins lining, reduces heavy bleeding Heavy bleeding with smaller fibroids; also provides contraception Tranexamic acid Reduces blood loss by helping clots form — non-hormonal Heavy bleeding; taken during period only GnRH agonists (injections) Temporarily shrink fibroids by stopping oestrogen — used before surgery Usually max 6 months; causes menopausal symptoms; fibroids often regrow after stopping Myomectomy Surgical removal of fibroids, preserving the uterus Women who still want children — fibroids can regrow. Done by keyhole or open surgery. Hysterectomy Complete removal of the uterus — permanently ends fibroids and heavy bleeding Severe symptoms when family is complete. Subtotal (cervix kept) or total (cervix removed). Uterine Artery Embolisation (UAE) Blocks blood supply to fibroids via a catheter — causes them to shrink. Done under local anaesthetic; 1–2 week recovery. Alternative to hysterectomy; pregnancy still possible but effects on fertility not fully understood Endometrial ablation Removes the lining of the womb — reduces heavy bleeding. ~20 minutes, day procedure. Not for women wanting future pregnancy — significant risks if pregnancy occurs after 🇰🇪 Visibility Matters — Janet Mbugua We celebrate Janet Mbugua, who openly shared her experience with fibroids, helping bring visibility to a condition many women silently endure. By speaking up, she created space for other women to voice their concerns boldly and feel seen, heard and validated. Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) PCOS is a hormonal disorder affecting how the ovaries work. It is one of the most common hormonal conditions in women of reproductive age — and it is both a reproductive and metabolic condition. It increases the long-term risk of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease. The Rotterdam Criteria — Diagnosis Needs 2 of 3 1. Irregular or absent ovulation (irregular periods) 2. Clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (excess hair growth, acne, or elevated testosterone on blood tests) 3. Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (12+ follicles in one ovary OR ovarian volume >10 mL) Note: Despite the name, you do not actually have \"cysts\" — the follicles are underdeveloped sacs in which eggs develop but cannot mature and release. Key Symptoms of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome - Irregular or absent periods (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea) - Difficulty conceiving (infertility due to lack of ovulation) - Excess facial or body hair (hirsutism) - Acne (especially lower face, chest, upper back) - Weight gain or difficulty losing weight, especially around the abdomen - Thinning hair on the scalp (male-pattern baldness) - Darkening of skin in folds (acanthosis nigricans) — neck, armpits, groin Why Insulin Resistance Matters in PCOS Many women with PCOS are resistant to insulin — their body produces extra amounts to compensate. High insulin stimulates the ovaries to produce more testosterone, disrupting normal ovulation and contributing to symptoms. Insulin resistance can also lead to weight gain, which further worsens the cycle by increasing insulin levels. Treatment Options for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Goal Treatment Notes First-line (all) Lifestyle modifications — as little as 5–10% weight loss can restore ovulation. Healthy diet, 150 min exercise/week, stress management, 6–8 hrs sleep. Most effective foundation for ALL PCOS management Irregular periods Combined contraceptive pill or intermittent progestogen — regulates periods and reduces long-term endometrial cancer risk Mirena IUS can also thin the lining without triggering regular bleeding Fertility Clomifene (first-line); letrozole; metformin (improves insulin resistance + ovulation); injectable gonadotrophins; IVF Metformin is NOT a weight loss drug — it targets insulin resistance specifically Excess hair/acne Combined pill; eflornithine cream (facial hair); anti-androgens (spironolactone — not in pregnancy); laser removal Anti-androgens require contraception as they can harm a male fetus Metabolic health GLP-1 agonists (Wegovy, Ozempic) for weight; cholesterol-lowering drugs; diabetes screening and management Regular screening for diabetes and cardiovascular risk is essential Surgery (fertility only) Laparoscopic ovarian drilling (LOD) — minor procedure reducing androgen-producing tissue in ovaries to restore ovulation Option when medications fail; lower multiple pregnancy risk than gonadotrophins 🇰🇪 Kenya Research Gap There are currently no Kenyan studies on the prevalence of PCOS in any population — meaning we have no data on how common it is in Kenya specifically. Given that up to 70% of global PCOS cases go undiagnosed, the true burden in Kenya is unknown. This is an area urgently needing research investment. Adenomyosis Adenomyosis is a condition where the lining of the uterus (endometrium) grows into the muscular wall of the uterus (myometrium), causing the uterus to become enlarged, boggy and tender. It can occur alongside endometriosis and shares many overlapping symptoms. Historically diagnosed only after hysterectomy — today high-quality transvaginal ultrasound and MRI can diagnose it in living patients. Symptoms of Adenomyosis Period-related: - Heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding - Severe cramping (sharp, stabbing pain during periods) Throughout the cycle: - Chronic pelvic pain - Pain during sex - Enlarged, tender uterus (felt on exam) - Bloating or pressure in lower abdomen Some people with adenomyosis have no symptoms at all. Diagnosis & Treatment Diagnosis: - Pelvic exam — enlarged, boggy, tender uterus - Transvaginal ultrasound — shows characteristic thickening of uterine wall - MRI — more detailed for complex cases Treatment: - NSAIDs and tranexamic acid for pain/bleeding - Mirena IUD — excellent for reducing bleeding and pain - Combined pill or GnRH agonists - Endometrial ablation - Hysterectomy — the only definitive cure; for severe cases when family is complete - Iron supplements if anaemic from heavy bleeding 💡 Key Diagnostic Clue If you have severe cramping and heavy bleeding, and an ultrasound shows an \"enlarged uterus\" but no fibroids — ask your provider: \"Could this be adenomyosis?\" It is frequently missed because it can appear as a vaguely enlarged uterus on routine scans. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) PID is an infection of the female upper reproductive tract — the uterus, fallopian tubes and ovaries. Usually caused by STIs like chlamydia and gonorrhoea, but can also result from other vaginal bacteria ascending upward. Many people with PID have no symptoms or only mild symptoms — and don't realise they have an infection until they have trouble conceiving. Symptoms of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease - Lower abdominal pain (dull or cramping between lower tummy and thighs) - Fever (sometimes) - Unusual vaginal discharge (yellow/green, foul-smelling) - Pain felt deep inside during sex - Painful and/or heavy periods (unusual for you) - Vaginal bleeding between periods or after sex Risk Factors - Sexually active women under 25 are at highest risk - Multiple partners or a partner with multiple partners - Prior history of PID or STIs - Having recently given birth, had a miscarriage, or had a termination - Having had an IUD fitted, hysteroscopy or any procedure that opens the cervix Treatment: Course of 2+ antibiotics covering multiple bacteria — often started immediately before test results return. Partner must also be treated to prevent reinfection. Complications of Untreated PID Complication What It Means Tubo-ovarian abscess Pus-filled swellings in the fallopian tubes or ovaries — can be life-threatening Chronic pelvic pain Long-term pain from scarring and adhesions in the pelvis Tubal factor infertility Scarring and blocking of tubes prevents egg and sperm meeting — accounts for up to 1/3 of infertility cases Ectopic pregnancy Damaged tubes increase risk of pregnancy implanting in the tube instead of the uterus — a medical emergency ⚠️ Go to Hospital Immediately If: - Severe pelvic pain getting worse or hurting when you move or touch the area - Pelvic pain with heavy vaginal bleeding - Sudden, sharp intense pain in lower abdomen - Pain under the ribs on the right side and in the right shoulder (may indicate spread) - Feeling dizzy or faint Gynaecological Cancers — Overview FIGO Staging — Universal System for All Gynaecological Cancers Stage I: Confined to the organ of origin. Stage II: Spread to nearby structures within the pelvis. Stage III: Spread to lymph nodes or other pelvic structures. Stage IV: Spread to distant organs (liver, lungs) or bladder/rectum. Grade 1 = slow-growing; Grade 3 = fast-growing. Together, stage and grade guide treatment and predict outcomes. Cervical Cancer — The One We Can Prevent - 5,845 new cases per year in Kenya - 3,286 deaths per year in Kenya - 14 Kenyan women die from cervical cancer daily Nearly all cervical cancers are caused by persistent high-risk HPV — a common virus transmitted through skin-to-skin sexual contact. Early stages: NO symptoms — which is why screening is essential. As cancer develops: - Abnormal vaginal bleeding (after sex, between periods, after menopause) - Watery or bloody vaginal discharge with foul odour - Pelvic pain or pain during intercourse - Pain when urinating Prevention — 90-70-90 Targets Kenya's National Cervical Cancer Elimination Action Plan 2026–2030 targets: - 90% of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15 - 70% of women screened using high-performance tests (HPV DNA) by ages 35 and 45 - 90% of women diagnosed receiving timely treatment HPV vaccine: Free at age 10 at public health facilities; single-dose (since November 2025); protects against HPV types causing 90% of cervical cancers plus 5 other cancers. 🇰🇪 Kenyan Science Behind Single-Dose HPV Vaccine The research establishing single-dose HPV vaccine efficacy — now adopted in 88 countries worldwide — was led by Kenyan women scientists: Dr. Nelly Mugo, Dr. Elizabeth Bukusi, Dr. Maricianah Onono and Dr. Betty Njoroge through the KENSHE study by KEMRI in collaboration with the University of Washington. Kenyan women scientists changed global vaccination policy. Uterine (Endometrial) Cancer Most common in postmenopausal women (average age at diagnosis: 63). Rates rising because of increased life expectancy, changing reproductive trends, rising obesity, and lack of awareness. Risk factors: obesity (BMI ≥31), unopposed estrogen (no progesterone), high blood pressure, Lynch syndrome, diabetes, late menopause (>55 years), tamoxifen use. The early warning sign: Abnormal bleeding — any postmenopausal bleeding (even spotting), heavy or prolonged bleeding in premenopausal women, or watery blood-tinged discharge. Up to 80% of endometrial cancers could be prevented if perimenopausal women with abnormal bleeding receive early intervention. Over 60% of uterine cancer patients in Kenya are diagnosed at advanced stages (III or IV). Don't wait — if you have any bleeding after menopause, see a provider immediately. Ovarian Cancer — Recognising the Subtle Signs Often called a \"silent killer\" because early symptoms are vague — but the symptoms ARE present, they are just subtle and easily dismissed. ~80% of patients are diagnosed at advanced stage. Kenya stats: ~1,245 new cases/year; ~895 deaths/year. Risk factors: Age >50; BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations (25% of cases); family history of breast/ovarian/colorectal cancer; endometriosis; nulliparity (never given birth); obesity. Symptoms of Ovarian Cancer — Persistent for >2 Weeks If these symptoms are new, persistent (lasting more than 2 weeks) and different from what you normally experience: - Bloating or increased abdominal size - Pelvic or abdominal pain/pressure - Difficulty eating or feeling full quickly (early satiety) - Urinary urgency or frequency - Fatigue, back pain, changes in bowel habits If BRCA mutation or strong family history: consider genetic counselling and discuss screening with your provider. Vulvar Cancer — Highly Curable When Caught Early Cancer beginning in the vulva (labia, clitoris, vaginal opening). Accounts for 5–8% of gynaecological malignancies. Kenya: ~200–250 cases/year; ~120 deaths/year. Median age: 68–70. Most are linked to HPV or chronic inflammation (lichen sclerosus). Look at your vulva regularly — because it's in a visible location, early detection is possible. Symptom Action Required A persistent lump or mass on the vulva (most common presentation) See a provider — requires biopsy to confirm diagnosis Persistent itching that doesn't go away Do not ignore — persistent pruritus always needs evaluation Non-healing ulcer or sore on the vulva Any sore that hasn't healed in 2–3 weeks must be evaluated Skin changes: thickening, colour change (red, white, darker) Especially if you have a history of lichen sclerosus — seek prompt review Bleeding not related to periods Requires immediate evaluation — do not wait Treatment & Support in Kenya Where to Seek Cancer Care - Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH) — National referral; comprehensive cancer care - Moi Teaching & Referral Hospital (MTRH) — Comprehensive cancer care - Nakuru Regional Cancer Centre — Regional care - Aga Khan University Hospital, MP Shah Hospital, Nairobi Hospital, Texas Cancer Hospital — Private sector Health Financing The Social Health Authority (SHA) has replaced NHIF.   "/health-library/womens-health/gynaecological-conditions/polycystic-ovary-syndrome": "Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) PCOS is a hormonal disorder affecting how the ovaries work. It is one of the most common hormonal conditions in women of reproductive age — and it is both a reproductive and metabolic condition. It increases the long-term risk of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease. The Rotterdam Criteria — Diagnosis Needs 2 of 3 1. Irregular or absent ovulation (irregular periods) 2. Clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (excess hair growth, acne, or elevated testosterone on blood tests) 3. Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (12+ follicles in one ovary OR ovarian volume >10 mL) Note: Despite the name, you do not actually have \"cysts\" — the follicles are underdeveloped sacs in which eggs develop but cannot mature and release. Key Symptoms of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome - Irregular or absent periods (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea) - Difficulty conceiving (infertility due to lack of ovulation) - Excess facial or body hair (hirsutism) - Acne (especially lower face, chest, upper back) - Weight gain or difficulty losing weight, especially around the abdomen - Thinning hair on the scalp (male-pattern baldness) - Darkening of skin in folds (acanthosis nigricans) — neck, armpits, groin Why Insulin Resistance Matters in PCOS Many women with PCOS are resistant to insulin — their body produces extra amounts to compensate. High insulin stimulates the ovaries to produce more testosterone, disrupting normal ovulation and contributing to symptoms. Insulin resistance can also lead to weight gain, which further worsens the cycle by increasing insulin levels. Treatment Options for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Goal Treatment Notes First-line (all) Lifestyle modifications — as little as 5–10% weight loss can restore ovulation. Healthy diet, 150 min exercise/week, stress management, 6–8 hrs sleep. Most effective foundation for ALL PCOS management Irregular periods Combined contraceptive pill or intermittent progestogen — regulates periods and reduces long-term endometrial cancer risk Mirena IUS can also thin the lining without triggering regular bleeding Fertility Clomifene (first-line); letrozole; metformin (improves insulin resistance + ovulation); injectable gonadotrophins; IVF Metformin is NOT a weight loss drug — it targets insulin resistance specifically Excess hair/acne Combined pill; eflornithine cream (facial hair); anti-androgens (spironolactone — not in pregnancy); laser removal Anti-androgens require contraception as they can harm a male fetus Metabolic health GLP-1 agonists (Wegovy, Ozempic) for weight; cholesterol-lowering drugs; diabetes screening and management Regular screening for diabetes and cardiovascular risk is essential Surgery (fertility only) Laparoscopic ovarian drilling (LOD) — minor procedure reducing androgen-producing tissue in ovaries to restore ovulation Option when medications fail; lower multiple pregnancy risk than gonadotrophins 🇰🇪 Kenya Research Gap There are currently no Kenyan studies on the prevalence of PCOS in any population — meaning we have no data on how common it is in Kenya specifically. They range from tiny seedlings to large masses distorting the uterus. Around 2 in 3 women develop at least one fibroid. Most likely to cause heavy bleeding and infertility. - Intramural: Grow within the muscular wall of the uterus — the most common type. - Subserosal: Grow on the outside of the uterus, projecting into the pelvis. Can cause pressure symptoms. - Pedunculated: Subserosal or submucosal fibroids on a stalk — can occasionally twist (torsion), causing acute pain. Key Symptoms of Uterine Fibroids Only 1 in 3 women have symptoms. - Heavy, prolonged menstrual bleeding — sometimes with large clots - Pelvic pressure and pain (feeling of fullness or heaviness) - Frequent urination (pressure on bladder) - Constipation (pressure on bowel) - Backache or leg pain - Pain during sex - Infertility or pregnancy complications (depending on location) Diagnosis Methods Test What It Shows Pelvic exam May reveal enlarged, irregularly shaped uterus Ultrasound (transvaginal or abdominal) Primary imaging tool — identifies fibroids, maps location, measures size Hysteroscopy Camera through vagina and cervix into womb — best for submucosal fibroids. Done by keyhole or open surgery. Hysterectomy Complete removal of the uterus — permanently ends fibroids and heavy bleeding Severe symptoms when family is complete. Subtotal (cervix kept) or total (cervix removed). Uterine Artery Embolisation (UAE) Blocks blood supply to fibroids via a catheter — causes them to shrink. Done under local anaesthetic; 1–2 week recovery. Alternative to hysterectomy; pregnancy still possible but effects on fertility not fully understood Endometrial ablation Removes the lining of the womb — reduces heavy bleeding. ~20 minutes, day procedure.   "/health-library/womens-health/hormones-life-stages/hormones-life-stages": "Hormones Across Life Stages Introduction: A Lifetime of Hormonal Change Your hormones are not static — they are a dynamic, living conversation between your brain and your body that changes across every stage of life. From the moment you are in your mother's womb, through puberty, your reproductive years and into menopause, these chemical messengers shape your health, your mood and your experience of being in the world. Hormonal changes are not something to fear — understanding them is the key to working with your body, not against it. 💡 The HPG Axis — The Master Control System The Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal (HPG) axis is the hormonal command chain: the hypothalamus (brain) releases GnRH in pulses → the pituitary gland responds with FSH and LH → the ovaries produce estrogen and progesterone → these feed back to regulate the brain. This sensitive system responds to stress, illness, sleep changes and exercise — which is why your cycle can change during difficult times. The 6 Key Hormones Estrogen (Estradiol) Source: Primarily ovaries; also fat tissue and adrenal glands. Role: Develops secondary sex characteristics at puberty; thickens uterine lining; maintains bone density; supports skin health, mood and cardiovascular function; dominant in the first half of the cycle (follicular phase). Levels: Peak at ovulation; decline sharply at menopause. Progesterone Source: Corpus luteum after ovulation; placenta during pregnancy. Role: Prepares the uterine lining for implantation; maintains early pregnancy; dominant in the second half of the cycle (luteal phase). Levels: Rise sharply after ovulation; if no pregnancy, collapse triggers menstruation; decline erratically in perimenopause. Testosterone Source: Ovaries and adrenal glands — yes, women produce testosterone naturally, just in smaller amounts than men. Role: Libido, mood, energy, muscle mass, bone health. Note: In women with PCOS, testosterone levels are often elevated, causing acne, facial hair growth and irregular ovulation. FSH — Follicle-Stimulating Hormone Source: Pituitary gland (in the brain). Role: Stimulates ovarian follicles to grow and mature at the start of each cycle. If no eggs remain (menopause), FSH rises dramatically as the pituitary tries harder and harder to stimulate ovaries that can no longer respond — elevated FSH is a marker of declining ovarian reserve. LH — Luteinising Hormone Source: Pituitary gland. Role: The mid-cycle LH surge (a sudden spike) triggers the dominant follicle to release a mature egg — this is ovulation. Ovulation predictor kits detect this surge. After ovulation, LH stimulates the ruptured follicle to become the corpus luteum, which then produces progesterone. Prolactin Source: Pituitary gland. Role: Primarily stimulates milk production after childbirth. High prolactin suppresses ovulation (which is why exclusive breastfeeding can temporarily prevent periods — the basis of LAM contraception). Note: Abnormally elevated prolactin outside of breastfeeding can cause irregular or absent periods and should be investigated. Hormones Across All 5 Life Stages Stage 1: In the Beginning — Fetal Development & Infancy In the Womb The absence of male sex hormones allows the female reproductive tract to develop. By the fifth month of gestation, a female fetus already has her lifetime supply of eggs — about 6–7 million, already formed in her ovaries. This number declines naturally throughout life. You are born with all the eggs you will ever have — a fixed, non-renewable resource. \"Minipuberty\" — First Few Months of Life Shortly after birth, there is a temporary activation of the HPG axis. This \"minipuberty\" helps solidify the development of the ovaries and external genitalia. It happens behind the scenes — no outward signs — but is a critical developmental window. From birth until puberty, the HPG axis is then relatively quiet: a period of \"rest\" before adolescence. Stage 2: Puberty & Adolescence (Ages 8–19) What Triggers Puberty The hypothalamus begins releasing GnRH in pulses, stimulating the pituitary to release FSH and LH. These signal the ovaries to produce estrogen. The adrenal glands also begin producing androgens (DHEA) years before puberty in a process called adrenarche — which triggers pubic and underarm hair growth independent of the ovaries. Early vs Late Puberty Concerns - Early puberty: Signs before age 8 should be evaluated — can indicate precocious puberty. - Delayed puberty: No breast development by age 13 requires evaluation. - Absent period: No period by age 15 (primary amenorrhea) requires evaluation. - Irregular cycles: Can take up to 5 years to regularise after menarche. By age 16, cycles should generally be predictable. ✨ Good to Know — Earlier Onset Over Time The age of puberty onset has been decreasing over the last 150 years, largely due to improved health and nutrition. Factors like moderate excess body weight can lead to earlier puberty, and genetics (mother's age at menarche) play a role. Stage 3: The Reproductive Years (Ages 20–39) Peak Fertility & the Monthly Rhythm The HPG axis is fully mature and functioning in a classic cyclical pattern. A predictable ebb and flow of estrogen and progesterone drives the monthly cycle. Peak fertility is in the 20s. Fertility begins a gradual decline in the 30s, with a more noticeable drop after age 35. A healthy 30-year-old has about a 20% chance of conceiving in any given cycle. By age 40, that drops to less than 5% per cycle. Egg Quality & Ovarian Reserve As a woman ages, so do her eggs. The risk of chromosomal abnormalities (like Down syndrome) and miscarriage increases because eggs are more likely to have abnormal chromosome numbers (aneuploidy). Tests like AMH (anti-müllerian hormone) and day-3 FSH can give an idea of ovarian reserve — but cannot perfectly predict the chance of pregnancy. ⚠️ Fertility Guidance - Under 35 years: Seek help after 1 year of regular, unprotected sex without conceiving - Ages 35–40: Seek help after 6 months - Over 40 years: Seek help immediately — do not wait Stage 4: The Perimenopause Transition (Ages 40–Early 50s) The Hormonal Rollercoaster Contrary to popular belief, perimenopause is not a steady decline in hormones — it is characterised by wild fluctuations. Estrogen levels may swing from very high to very low unpredictably. Progesterone production becomes erratic as ovulation becomes less consistent. This volatility, not just low estrogen, causes many classic symptoms. The transition typically lasts 2–8 years, beginning in the 40s. Cycle Changes The first sign is often a shortening of the menstrual cycle (cycles become 21–25 days apart). Later, cycles become longer and more irregular, with skipped periods. As the pool of ovarian follicles dwindles, the restraints on follicular growth (inhibin B and AMH) are lifted, leading to a final \"burst\" of follicular activity before the end. Symptom Category What You Might Experience Vasomotor Hot flashes, night sweats (affect up to 80% of women). Caused by estrogen fluctuations affecting the brain's temperature regulation centre. Sleep Difficulty falling asleep and staying asleep — often linked to night sweats disrupting rest cycles Mood Irritability, mood swings, anxiety (can feel like severe PMS). A Feb 2026 review in Biological Psychiatry confirms estradiol fluctuations impact brain neurotransmitters (serotonin, dopamine, GABA), directly affecting mood. Cognitive Trouble concentrating, \"brain fog,\" memory lapses — often temporary and related to sleep disruption and hormone fluctuations Physical Vaginal dryness (early sign), joint and muscle aches, headaches, skin changes, hair thinning 💡 You Can Still Get Pregnant During Perimenopause Ovulation is erratic but not impossible during perimenopause. Continue using contraception until you have gone 12 full months without a period. Do not assume you cannot conceive just because your periods are irregular. Stage 5: Menopause & Beyond (Ages 50+) Definition & Timeline Menopause is defined as 12 consecutive months without a period. Average age: 52 years (typical range 46–55). With average life expectancy now over 65 in Kenya, most women will spend over one-third of their lives in the postmenopausal stage. Smoking can cause menopause about a year earlier. Long-Term Effects of Low Estrogen - Bone: Estrogen maintains bone density — its loss accelerates bone loss (osteoporosis risk). - Heart: Estrogen protects the cardiovascular system — risk of heart disease and high cholesterol increases. - Genitourinary: Vaginal tissues thin, dry and lose elasticity (GSM). - Brain: Increased focus on cognitive health and dementia prevention strategies. ⚠️ Any Bleeding After Menopause is NOT Normal Any bleeding after 12+ months without a period requires urgent medical evaluation. It could be a sign of endometrial (uterine) cancer or other serious conditions. Do not wait — even a single episode of spotting after menopause warrants immediate assessment. Which Stage Am I In? — Quick Reference Your Situation Likely Stage What to Do Under 8 with no body changes yet Pre-pubertal Normal. Evaluate if over 13 with no breast development. Ages 8–19, periods starting or irregular Puberty / Adolescence Irregular cycles common for 1–2 years. Seek help if: periods extremely heavy, pain debilitating, or no period by age 15. Ages 20–39 with regular periods Reproductive Years Track your cycle. Seek fertility help after 1 year trying (or 6 months if over 35). Ages 40–50 with changing cycles or new hot flashes Perimenopause Normal. Track symptoms. Use contraception — you can still conceive. Seek help if symptoms are severe or bleeding is very heavy. Over 50 with no period for over 1 year Postmenopause Focus on bone health, heart health and managing ongoing symptoms. ANY bleeding is not normal — seek urgent evaluation. When to Seek Medical Help at Any Stage - No period by age 15 (Primary Amenorrhea) - Periods stop for 3+ months when not pregnant (Secondary Amenorrhea) - Bleeding is extremely heavy — soaking a pad/tampon every hour - Bleeding between periods or after sex - Severe, debilitating pain that OTC medication does not help - Sudden, severe pelvic pain (could be ectopic pregnancy or ovarian cyst rupture) - Any bleeding after menopause — URGENT - Severe mood symptoms that interfere with daily life (depression, anxiety, rage) - Fever with pelvic pain",

  "/health-library/womens-health/menopause-perimenopause/long-term-health-after-menopause": "Part 6: Long-Term Health After Menopause With lower estrogen levels, certain health risks increase after menopause. Being proactive — starting lifestyle changes well before menopause — can make a significant difference to long-term outcomes. Start building bone and heart health NOW, at whatever age you are reading this. Health Area What Changes What to Do ------------ ------------ ----------- 🦴 Bone Health Estrogen maintains bone density. After menopause, bone loss accelerates — increasing risk of osteoporosis and fractures (especially hip, wrist, shoulder). The first 5 years after menopause see the fastest bone loss. Adequate calcium intake; Vitamin D (sunlight + supplements); weight-bearing exercise (walking, jogging, dancing); strength and resistance training; bone density screening (DEXA scan); medications if needed (bisphosphonates, denosumab). Start these habits in your 20s and 30s. ❤️ Heart Health Estrogen has a protective effect on the cardiovascular system. After menopause, risk of heart disease, high cholesterol and stroke increases. Heart disease is the leading cause of death in postmenopausal women. Monitor blood pressure and cholesterol regularly; heart-healthy diet (low salt, healthy fats, lots of vegetables); regular aerobic exercise; do not smoke or vape; manage stress; control diabetes and blood pressure if present. 🧠 Brain Health The February 2026 estradiol review highlights estrogen's importance for brain function. Brain fog during perimenopause is common — usually temporary. Long-term, managing vascular risk factors is key for cognitive health. Stay mentally active (reading, learning, puzzles); social engagement; physical activity; manage blood pressure, diabetes and other chronic conditions. HRT is not recommended solely for cognitive protection. 🌸 Pelvic Floor Health Years after menopause, pelvic floor issues may emerge: pelvic organ prolapse (bladder, uterus or bowel descending into vagina) and urinary incontinence become more common. Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels) — do them daily, starting well before menopause; maintain healthy weight; treat constipation (straining worsens prolapse); seek pelvic floor physiotherapy if available; vaginal oestrogen helps maintain pelvic tissue health. Myth-Busting: Menopause ❌ Myth ✅ Truth \"Menopause means you are old and your life is over\" Menopause marks the end of fertility, not the end of vitality. Many women enter their most vibrant, productive decades after menopause. In Kenya, with average life expectancy now over 65, you may live one-third of your life after menopause — make it count. \"Menopause symptoms are just something women must endure\" While menopause is natural, severe symptoms are treatable. Combined HRT slightly increases breast cancer risk with long-term use (5+ years), but the absolute risk is small. Estrogen-only therapy (for women without a uterus) shows little to no increased breast cancer risk.   "/health-library/womens-health/menopause-perimenopause/menopause-perimenopause": "Menopause & Perimenopause Introduction: A Natural Transition, A New Understanding Menopause is not a disease or a deficiency — it is a natural biological transition marking the end of the reproductive years. Yet for decades it has been shrouded in silence, stigma and outdated information. That is now changing in a landmark way. The median age for menopause is 52, with most women experiencing it between 45 and 55. With increasing life expectancy, women now spend approximately one-third of their lives in the postmenopausal stage — making understanding this transition more important than ever. 🚨 Breaking News · November 2025 FDA Approves Historic Hormone Therapy Label Changes In November 2025, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved sweeping changes to hormone therapy labels — removing decades-old \"black box\" warnings that had frightened millions of women away from treatment since 2002. This is the most significant update in menopause medicine in over 20 years. These changes reflect updated science and the \"timing hypothesis.\" See Part 4 below for full details. Part 1: Perimenopause — The Years Before Perimenopause, meaning \"around menopause,\" is the transitional period leading up to menopause. It typically begins in the 40s but can start as early as the mid-30s. It can last 4–8 years. Contrary to popular belief, it is not a steady decline — it is characterised by wild hormonal fluctuations. What Happens Hormonally - Estrogen levels swing wildly — from very high to very low unpredictably - Progesterone production becomes erratic as ovulation becomes less consistent - Cycles may shorten first (21–25 days) then lengthen and become irregular with skipped periods - The pool of ovarian follicles nears exhaustion — as they dwindle, restraints on follicular growth (inhibin B and AMH) are lifted, leading to a final \"burst\" of follicular activity before the end - This volatility — not just low estrogen — causes many classic symptoms New Research: Estrogen & Depression Risk A groundbreaking February 2026 review in Biological Psychiatry reveals that it is the fluctuations in estradiol (the most neuroactive form of estrogen) — not just low levels — that may trigger depression risk in vulnerable women during perimenopause. Mechanisms identified: - Neurotransmitter signalling — estrogen affects serotonin, dopamine and GABA - Neuroimmune function — inflammation may play a role - Brain glucose metabolism — energy supply to brain cells - Synaptogenesis — formation of connections between neurons 💡 You Can Still Get Pregnant During Perimenopause Ovulation is erratic but not impossible. Continue using contraception until you have gone 12 full consecutive months without a period. The average age of menopause is 52 — factors like smoking can bring it about a year earlier. Part 2: Menopause — The Milestone Official Definition Menopause is officially defined as the point when you have gone 12 consecutive months without a period. At this point, the ovaries have largely ceased producing estrogen and progesterone, and ovulation no longer occurs. Average age: 52 years (range: typically 46–55) Premature menopause (&lt;40): Called Primary Ovarian Insufficiency — requires evaluation and usually hormone therapy STRAW+10 Staging System The gold standard for defining reproductive stages: - Reproductive: Regular cycles, fertile (menarche to 40s) - Early perimenopause: Variable cycles, ≤7 days difference from normal (40s) - Late perimenopause: ≥60 days of no periods, fluctuating hormones (late 40s–early 50s) - Early postmenopause: First 5–8 years after final period (50s) - Late postmenopause: Beyond 8 years after final period (60+) ✨ Induced Menopause Some women experience induced menopause from surgery (hysterectomy with ovary removal), chemotherapy or radiation. This sudden drop in hormones can cause more severe and sudden symptoms than natural menopause, as the body has no time to gradually adjust. Women experiencing induced menopause before 45 are particularly vulnerable to long-term health effects and should discuss hormone therapy with their provider. Part 3: Symptoms — What to Expect Up to 75% of women experience hot flashes · 20% report severe symptoms I. Vasomotor Symptoms — Hot Flashes & Night Sweats Feature Description What it feels like Sudden sensation of intense heat, often in the face, neck and chest; may cause flushing, sweating and skin reddening Duration Usually 1–5 minutes, but can last longer; frequency varies from a few per week to many per day Common triggers Hot drinks, spicy food, alcohol, stress, warm environments, tight clothing Night sweats Hot flashes during sleep — drench pyjamas and sheets; disrupt sleep cycles causing daytime fatigue and mood disturbance Duration of symptoms On average, vasomotor symptoms last 7–10 years. For about 10–15% of women, they persist indefinitely. Research shows Black women often experience more severe and longer-lasting vasomotor symptoms (SWAN study). II. Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause (GSM) This term encompasses vaginal and urinary symptoms caused by estrogen loss — affecting up to 45% of postmenopausal women. Unlike hot flashes which often lessen over time, GSM is progressive without treatment. Many women are too embarrassed to discuss these symptoms — but effective treatments exist. Vaginal Symptoms - Vaginal dryness, itching and burning - Pain during sex (dyspareunia) - Increased susceptibility to vaginal infections - Decreased natural lubrication during arousal This does not mean your sex life is over — effective treatments exist. You should not \"just tolerate\" painful sex. Urinary Symptoms - Urinary urgency (sudden strong need to go) - Urinary frequency (needing to go often) - Recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) - Urinary leakage with urgency (urge incontinence) Low-dose vaginal estrogen can dramatically improve all these symptoms — with minimal systemic absorption. III. Other Common Symptoms Category Symptoms Sleep Insomnia, night sweats, difficulty staying asleep — one of the most distressing symptoms for many women. Sleep deprivation worsens mood, cognition and physical symptoms. Mood Irritability, mood swings, anxiety, increased depression risk (see February 2026 estradiol research). Can feel like severe PMS. Does not mean you are \"going mad.\" Cognitive \"Brain fog\" — difficulty concentrating, memory lapses, word-finding difficulties. Often temporary and related to sleep disruption and hormone fluctuations. Usually improves with adequate sleep and treatment. Physical Joint aches and muscle pain (many women are surprised by this); headaches; weight gain — especially around the middle; dry skin; thinning hair; brittle nails ⚠️ Not Everything Is Menopause Not every symptom in your 40s and 50s is caused by menopause. Thyroid disorders, vitamin deficiencies, depression, anaemia and other conditions can mimic menopause symptoms. Always get a thorough evaluation — do not assume everything is \"just the menopause\" without investigation. Part 4: The 2025 FDA Landmark Changes The Most Significant Update in Menopause Medicine in 20+ Years Before November 2025 After November 2025 Black box warnings for cardiovascular disease, breast cancer and probable dementia on all HRT products These warnings removed from prescribing information — replaced with updated, nuanced guidance Strong warnings based entirely on the 2002 Women's Health Initiative (WHI) study Updated warnings now reflect current science and the \"timing hypothesis\" Millions of women and doctors avoided HRT even when clearly appropriate and beneficial More women can now consider HRT as a safe option — estimated only 2 million of 41 million eligible US women received a prescription in 2020 Why Did This Change Happen? The Study's Critical Flaw The WHI studied mostly older women (average age 63 — many a decade past menopause onset). The risks observed in this older group do not apply to women who start HRT within 10 years of menopause onset. The Timing Hypothesis Women who start HRT within 10 years of menopause or before age 60 have a very different (more favourable) risk profile than women starting later. For this group, cardiovascular benefits may actually exist. What Remains The warning for endometrial cancer remains on systemic estrogen-alone therapies. Women with a uterus must still take progestogen alongside estrogen to protect the uterine lining. Individual risk assessment remains essential. 🇰🇪 Kenya Context The FDA changes apply to US-approved hormone therapy products. In Kenya, the Pharmacy and Poisons Board may take time to update local labelling. However, the scientific consensus has shifted globally — Kenyan providers can and should prescribe based on current evidence. If you have avoided HRT due to fear of the \"old\" warnings, now is the time for a fresh conversation with your healthcare provider about your personal risk. Part 5: Treatment Options — What's Available Now 1. Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT / MHT) The most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and genitourinary syndrome of menopause. Involves taking estrogen (and progestogen for those with a uterus) to replace what the ovaries no longer make. Type What It Is For Whom Estrogen-only therapy Estrogen alone (systemic) Women who have had a hysterectomy — no risk of endometrial cancer without a uterus Combined therapy (E+P) Estrogen + progestogen — the progestogen protects the uterine lining Women with an intact uterus — essential to prevent endometrial cancer Low-dose vaginal estrogen Creams, tablets, rings applied or inserted vaginally Women with only vaginal/urinary symptoms — minimal systemic absorption; extremely safe even in most breast cancer survivors Routes of Administration Route Forms Key Advantage Oral (tablets) Pills taken daily Convenient, widely available — but passes through the liver (higher blood clot risk than transdermal) Transdermal (through skin) Patches, gels, sprays applied to skin Avoids first-pass liver metabolism — lower blood clot and stroke risk than oral HRT; preferred for women with clot risk Subcutaneous implant/pellet Small pellet inserted under skin of abdomen or buttock — lasts 4–8 months (may continue releasing up to 18–24 months) Consistent hormone levels without daily attention; useful when other methods are ineffective Vaginal (local only) Creams, tablets, rings Local effect only — minimal systemic absorption; recommended specifically for GSM symptoms Benefits vs Risks of HRT Benefits - Most effective relief for hot flashes and night sweats - Prevents bone loss and fractures (osteoporosis) - Improves vaginal health and sexual function - Improves sleep and mood - When started within 10 years of menopause, may reduce all-cause mortality - A Jan 2026 study in Life Sciences shows estrogen protects the heart, aorta and kidneys by activating cellular \"cleaning\" (autophagy) through estrogen receptors Risks (Context-Dependent) - Small increased risk of breast cancer with combined (E+P) therapy — duration-dependent; less with estrogen-only - Small increased risk of ovarian cancer (becomes apparent within 5 years; diminishes after stopping) - Oral HRT increases blood clot/pulmonary embolism risk — transdermal does not - HRT does not prevent heart disease or cognitive decline and should not be prescribed solely for these purposes - Individual risk assessment is always essential 2. Non-Hormonal Prescription Medications Medication How It Works Notes Elinzanatant (Lynkuet) Approved November 2025 Blocks Neurokinin 1 (NK1) and Neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptors in the brain that regulate body temperature. A completely new non-hormonal mechanism of action. For women who cannot or prefer not to take hormones. Side effects: fatigue, dizziness, drowsiness. May actually improve sleep as a side effect. SSRIs/SNRIs (antidepressants) e.g., paroxetine, venlafaxine Reduce frequency and severity of hot flashes — off-label use Also beneficial for perimenopausal depression. Not all SSRIs are equally effective for hot flashes. Gabapentin Reduces hot flash frequency — off-label use Particularly useful for night sweats; can cause dizziness and drowsiness Ospemifene (SERM) A selective estrogen receptor modulator for vaginal dryness and painful sex — taken as a daily tablet An option for women who cannot use vaginal estrogen Vaginal moisturisers/lubricants Maintain vaginal moisture and reduce friction during sex First-line treatment for GSM. Non-hormonal — can be used by anyone. Hyaluronic acid gels show comparable efficacy to vaginal estrogen in some studies. 3. Lifestyle Approaches Cooling Strategies & Triggers - Dress in layers to easily remove when hot - Use fans or cool water on your face and neck - Keep your bedroom cool for sleep - Common triggers to avoid: hot drinks, spicy food, alcohol, caffeine, stress, warm environments Exercise, Diet & Mind-Body - Regular physical activity — improves mood, sleep, bone health and cardiovascular health - Diet: Work with a dietitian; moderate caffeine and alcohol; phytoestrogens (soy, flaxseed) — mixed evidence but generally safe - Stress management: Yoga, meditation, deep breathing, CBT - Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels): Help with urinary symptoms and vaginal tone Part 6: Long-Term Health After Menopause With lower estrogen levels, certain health risks increase after menopause. Being proactive — starting lifestyle changes well before menopause — can make a significant difference to long-term outcomes. Start building bone and heart health NOW, at whatever age you are reading this. Health Area What Changes What to Do 🦴 Bone Health Estrogen maintains bone density. After menopause, bone loss accelerates — increasing risk of osteoporosis and fractures (especially hip, wrist, shoulder). The first 5 years after menopause see the fastest bone loss. Adequate calcium intake; Vitamin D (sunlight + supplements); weight-bearing exercise (walking, jogging, dancing); strength and resistance training; bone density screening (DEXA scan); medications if needed (bisphosphonates, denosumab). Start these habits in your 20s and 30s. ❤️ Heart Health Estrogen has a protective effect on the cardiovascular system. After menopause, risk of heart disease, high cholesterol and stroke increases. Heart disease is the leading cause of death in postmenopausal women. Monitor blood pressure and cholesterol regularly; heart-healthy diet (low salt, healthy fats, lots of vegetables); regular aerobic exercise; do not smoke or vape; manage stress; control diabetes and blood pressure if present. 🧠 Brain Health The February 2026 estradiol review highlights estrogen's importance for brain function. Brain fog during perimenopause is common — usually temporary. Long-term, managing vascular risk factors is key for cognitive health. Stay mentally active (reading, learning, puzzles); social engagement; physical activity; manage blood pressure, diabetes and other chronic conditions. HRT is not recommended solely for cognitive protection. 🌸 Pelvic Floor Health Years after menopause, pelvic floor issues may emerge: pelvic organ prolapse (bladder, uterus or bowel descending into vagina) and urinary incontinence become more common. Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels) — do them daily, starting well before menopause; maintain healthy weight; treat constipation (straining worsens prolapse); seek pelvic floor physiotherapy if available; vaginal oestrogen helps maintain pelvic tissue health. Part 7: Emerging Research — The Future of Menopause Care Estrogen Receptor-Autophagy Axis (Jan 2026) A January 2026 study in Life Sciences reveals a previously unknown mechanism: estrogen protects the heart, aorta and kidneys by activating autophagy (cellular \"cleaning\") through estrogen receptors. This research opens new targets for therapy and confirms estrogen's organ-protective effects beyond just symptom relief. Regenerative Research — Experimental Areas under active research (not yet available for routine use): - Stem cell transplantation — regenerating ovarian tissue - Intraovarian PRP (platelet-rich plasma) — rejuvenating ovarian function - Ovarian tissue cryopreservation — preserving fertility or delaying menopause - Telomerase activators — potentially slowing cellular ovarian aging - Metabolic modulators (metformin, rapamycin) — under study for ovarian aging 💡 The Goal These innovations aim not just to extend fertility but to preserve endocrine health, enhance quality of life and promote healthy aging. The field of \"reproductive longevity\" is emerging as a recognised area of medicine — pointing toward a future where the postmenopausal years can be actively managed for optimal health.
